audio.t: Harbourlight Outdoor Centre, Mei speaking. How can I help?
Hello. I saw your advert for the two-day sea kayaking weekend and I would like to book a place.
Certainly. Can I take your surname first?
It is Natarajan. That is N-A-T-A-R-A-J-A-N.
Thank you. We have two weekends left. The first is the eleventh of July, and the second leaves on the eighteenth of July.
The eleventh is too early for me, because I am away. The eighteenth of July would suit me better.
Lovely. Now, have you paddled on the sea before? We ask because the trip is graded, and I see it says intermediate on the website.
I have only paddled on a lake, so I would call myself a beginner. Is that a problem?
Not at all. The coach will group you with other beginners, and you will have a short lesson on the first morning.
Good. Where do we meet?
At the Lantern car park, by the harbour wall. Please do not go to the main centre, which is a few miles away. Be there at eight thirty.
Lantern car park, got it. How much is it?
It is two hundred and ten dollars normally, but there is a discount for early booking, so it comes to one hundred and eighty-five dollars per person.
That is fine. How many people will be in the group?

We take a maximum of six, so you will get plenty of attention. Now, about equipment. We provide the kayaks, life jackets and spray decks. You need to bring warm clothes, sun cream, and a torch, because we walk to the beach camp after dark on the first evening.
A torch. Right. I should also mention that I am vegetarian.
That is no problem. We will note it down. Meals are cooked on the beach by the guides.
Where do we sleep? Is it the bunkhouse?
The bunkhouse is full that weekend, I am afraid. You will be sleeping in a tent. We supply those as well, and they are very comfortable.
That sounds like fun.
Finally, could I have a mobile number in case the weather forces us to change plans?
Yes, it is zero seven seven zero zero, four eight one, nine three six.
Zero seven seven zero zero, four eight one, nine three six. Thank you, Mr Natarajan. I will send a confirmation email today.

parts.instr: Listen to a talk about a new community project and answer the questions.
parts.instrVi: Nghe bài nói về một dự án cộng đồng mới và trả lời các câu hỏi.

audio.t: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming to this preview of the Newbridge Tool Library. I am Helen Okafor, and I coordinate the project. People often assume we are a shop, which we are not. Members borrow tools, from drills and ladders to sewing machines, in the same way they would borrow books from a library.

The idea began three years ago, when a group of residents noticed that most households own a drill that is used for perhaps ten minutes in its whole life. A survey of two hundred homes confirmed it, and it showed something we did not expect. The main reason people did not do repairs was not cost, and it was not lack of time. It was that they did not have the right equipment.

We had originally hoped to open in the old town hall, but the building needed a new roof, so we have taken the former bus depot on Foundry Road instead. It is bigger, and it has a workshop at the back. There is no car park, though, so please plan to cycle or take the number twelve bus.

Membership costs twenty dollars a year, but it is free for anyone under eighteen. Members can borrow up to three items at a time, for one week, and renew once. Late returns are not charged. Instead, a member loses borrowing rights for as many days as the item was late. In our pilot scheme, that worked better than fines.

We now hold about four hundred items. In the pilot, the most requested was not a power tool but a steam wallpaper stripper, followed by ladders. Anything with a motor requires a short induction session on a member's first visit. It takes about thirty minutes and is run by a volunteer electrician.

The project is funded by a lottery grant that covers the first two years of rent. A local hardware store gave us all the shelving, which is why the shelves do not match. After two years, we hope to cover our costs through membership and by running paid workshops for the public.

On Thursday evenings we will run a repair session, where people bring broken toasters, lamps or bicycles and volunteers help them fix them. We are still short of volunteers, particularly people who can repair textiles. If that is you, please speak to Anil at the front desk after this talk. Finally, we open this Saturday at nine o'clock.

Residents noticed that tools were rarely used.

parts.instr: Listen to two students discussing a research project with their tutor and answer the questions.
parts.instrVi: Nghe hai sinh viên thảo luận dự án nghiên cứu với giảng viên và trả lời các câu hỏi.

audio.t: Come in, both of you. So, your proposal is to compare surface temperatures on tree-lined and treeless streets in the Ashby district.
That's right. We planned to survey four streets, two with trees and two without.

Four is too few, I am afraid. With only four, you could not separate the effect of the trees from the effect of street orientation. A street running east to west gets sun in a different pattern from one running north to south. I would aim for at least eight, matched in pairs by orientation.
Eight streets means a lot of readings. We were hoping to borrow the thermal camera from the engineering department, but they only lend it for a week.

A camera is accurate, but a week will not cover eight streets. Use handheld infrared thermometers for the bulk of the readings. They are less precise, but you can take hundreds. Then borrow the camera for a single day and use it to check that your thermometers are reading correctly.
That makes sense. We were thinking of measuring at noon, when the sun is highest.

Noon is not ideal. Pavements store heat, so the hottest surface temperatures usually come in the middle of the afternoon. That is when the contrast between shaded and unshaded streets will be strongest.
What about the weather? If we only go out on sunny days, we might wait for weeks.
You do not need to wait for perfect days. Go out in any dry conditions, but record the cloud cover each time, and take it into account when you analyse the data.
Do we need ethics approval to take measurements? We are not interviewing anyone.

No, because no people are involved, and the pavements are public. What you do need is a risk assessment, because you will be working beside traffic. Please hand that in before you start any fieldwork.
We found a review of forty studies on urban cooling by trees, which seemed ideal.
It is a useful starting point, but notice that most of the studies were carried out in hot, dry climates. Our city is temperate, so you should say clearly that the findings may not transfer.
Right. For the analysis, we thought we would just calculate the average temperature difference between the two kinds of street.

audio.t: Today I want to look at bioluminescence, the production of light by living organisms, and in particular its role in the deep sea. Let us begin with the chemistry. Light is produced when a molecule called luciferin is oxidised, and the reaction is speeded up by an enzyme known as luciferase. Different species use different luciferins, which is one of the reasons we think the ability has arisen independently at least forty times in the history of life.

Now, the colour. Most marine bioluminescence is blue. That is not an accident. Blue light travels farthest in seawater, because water absorbs the longer red and yellow wavelengths much more quickly. An animal that flashes blue can therefore be seen from a greater distance than one that flashes any other colour.

What is the light for? One answer is camouflage, and the technique has a name: counter-illumination. In the dim twilight zone, a predator looking upward sees animals as dark silhouettes against the faint light from the surface. Some animals avoid this by producing light themselves, matching the brightness of the water above them, so the silhouette disappears. The hatchet fish does this with rows of light organs on its belly.
A second use is predation. The anglerfish carries a glowing lure on a stalk above its mouth. Small animals are drawn towards it, and then the anglerfish simply opens its jaws and takes its prey.

A third use is defence. When a dinoflagellate, a microscopic plankton cell, is disturbed by water movement, it flashes. One hypothesis for this is called the burglar alarm. The flash does not frighten the attacker. Instead, it attracts a larger predator, which then eats the attacker, so the flash makes the dinoflagellate's own situation safer.

Finally, I should mention that not every animal wants to be seen by everyone. The dragonfish produces red light, which almost no deep-sea animals can detect. It can therefore light up its surroundings like a torch without alerting its prey, giving it a kind of private channel.

parts.instr: Read the passage and answer questions 1-13.
parts.instrVi: Đọc đoạn văn và trả lời câu hỏi 1-13.

items.text:
A. Every science begins by asking why, yet philosophers have never agreed on what a satisfying answer looks like. A child who asks why the sky is dark at night is not requesting a prediction, since she already knows that it will be dark tomorrow. Nor is she asking for a description, since she can see the darkness for herself. She wants something that makes the fact intelligible: a reason why it had to be so, or at least why it should not surprise her. The philosophy of scientific explanation is the attempt to say what that something is, and to say it in a way that separates genuine explanations from the pseudo-explanations that merely sound authoritative.

B. The most influential twentieth-century proposal held that to explain an event is to show that it was to be expected. On this covering-law view, an explanation is an argument. Its premises include at least one general law of nature, together with a statement of the relevant initial conditions, and its conclusion is a description of the event to be explained. The attraction of the account was that it made explanation respectable. It required no mysterious necessary connections in nature, only laws and logic, and it treated explanation and prediction as two sides of one coin. An explanation was simply a prediction made after the event, and a prediction was an explanation offered in advance.

C. Critics soon produced counterexamples that the model could neither accommodate nor reject. In the best known, the length of a flagpole's shadow can be derived from the height of the pole, the angle of the sun and the laws of optics, and the derivation looks like a perfectly good explanation. But the height of the pole can equally be derived from the length of the shadow, the angle of the sun and the same laws, and nobody believes that the shadow explains how tall the pole is. The covering-law view therefore counts as explanatory an argument that intuition rejects, because it has no means of registering that explanation runs in one direction only. A second family of cases shows that an argument can satisfy every formal requirement and still rely on irrelevant facts. Salt that has been hexed by a magician will dissolve in water, and the premises that all hexed salt dissolves in water and that this sample was hexed entail the outcome flawlessly. Yet the hexing explains nothing, since the salt would have dissolved regardless.

D. Many philosophers concluded that what the covering-law model lacked was causation. On causal accounts, to explain an event is to locate it in the web of causes that produced it. The shadow does not explain the pole's height because shadows are effects of poles and not the reverse, and the hexing is idle because it makes no causal difference to dissolving. Mechanistic versions of the approach emphasise the parts and operations whose organisation produces a phenomenon. To explain how a cell divides is to describe its machinery, not to subsume division under a law. Such accounts fit biology and neuroscience, where exceptionless laws are scarce, far better than the covering-law model ever did. A related interventionist idea holds that a good explanation identifies factors which, if they were altered by an idealised manipulation, would change the outcome, and thereby ties explanation to what-if questions.

E. Yet causal accounts face a stubborn residue. Some scientific explanations appear not to cite causes at all. Why is it impossible to cross each of the seven bridges of a certain old city exactly once in a single walk? The answer lies in the structure of the network, in the mathematical fact that such a walk requires at most two landmasses to be joined by an odd number of bridges. It does not lie in any event that caused walkers to fail. Some defenders of causal views reply that such answers are not scientific explanations at all but mathematical demonstrations of impossibility. Their opponents insist that the distinction is a convenient fiction, and that a broader notion is needed: one that covers any account showing how a phenomenon depends on the structure of what is possible.

F. A rival tradition holds that explanation is unification. We understand more, on this view, when a single pattern of argument is shown to cover a wide range of apparently unrelated phenomena. Newton's mechanics, for instance, accounted for tides, planetary orbits and falling apples with a handful of principles. The best explanatory system is the one that derives the largest number of observations from the smallest stock of argument patterns, and the proposal elegantly accounts for the premium scientists place on theories that do more with less. Its weakness, critics say, is that unification can be bought cheaply, by gerrymandering the patterns, and that it does not obviously respect the direction of explanation that the flagpole case exposed.

G. A more deflationary stance denies that explanation is a relation between a theory and a fact at all, and treats it instead as an act performed in a context. The question of why a bridge collapsed, asked by an engineer, an insurance assessor and a historian, calls for three different answers, each of them correct. According to pragmatic accounts, what counts as explanatory depends on the contrast class implied by the question: why this rather than that? The logical form of the answer matters less than whether it addresses the contrast the questioner has in mind. Opponents reply that pragmatics cannot be the whole story. Context may select among explanations, but it does not create the facts that make them true.

H. Most philosophers today are pluralists of some kind, and recent attention has turned to idealisation. Scientific models routinely falsify their targets deliberately, assuming frictionless planes, infinite populations or perfectly rational agents, and yet they appear to explain. Some argue that such models succeed by isolating the factors that make a difference, so that falsehood in the details is harmless. The debate remains unresolved, but it has refined the question. Few now ask what the single form of explanation is. The more pressing question is what, if anything, the varied explanatory practices of science have in common.

items.q: A child who asks why the sky is dark at night is chiefly asking for a prediction.
items.vi: Đoạn A: em bé đã biết trước bầu trời sẽ tối nên không cần dự đoán; điều em muốn là sự giải thích.

items.q: The covering-law view treats explanation and prediction as logically equivalent in structure.
items.vi: Đoạn B: giải thích là dự đoán đưa ra sau sự kiện, dự đoán là giải thích đưa ra trước.

items.q: The flagpole example shows that a valid derivation can reverse the real direction of explanation.
items.vi: Đoạn C: chiều cao cột có thể suy ra từ bóng và ngược lại, nhưng bóng không giải thích chiều cao.

items.q: Mechanistic accounts of explanation were first developed by neuroscientists rather than philosophers.
items.vi: Bài không nói ai đã phát triển thuyết cơ chế đầu tiên.

items.q: Some defenders of causal accounts deny that the bridge-walk answer is a scientific explanation.
items.vi: Đoạn E: một số người bảo vệ thuyết nhân quả cho rằng đó chỉ là chứng minh toán học về điều bất khả thi.

items.q: Philosophers today overwhelmingly favour a single causal account of explanation.
items.vi: Đoạn H: đa số hiện nay theo chủ nghĩa đa nguyên, không phải một thuyết nhân quả duy nhất.

items.q: Why does the author begin with the example of a child?

items.text:
A. Since the beginning of the industrial era, the oceans have absorbed roughly a quarter of the carbon dioxide released by human activity. This service has slowed atmospheric warming, but at a chemical cost. When carbon dioxide dissolves in seawater, it reacts with water to form carbonic acid, which releases hydrogen ions. Average surface pH has fallen by about 0.1 units since the late eighteenth century. Because the pH scale is logarithmic, that apparently trivial change corresponds to a rise of around 30 percent in the concentration of hydrogen ions. The term acidification is, strictly speaking, a little misleading. Seawater remains alkaline and is merely becoming less so, and many chemists prefer to emphasise a second consequence of the reaction.

B. The additional hydrogen ions combine with carbonate ions and convert them to bicarbonate. Carbonate is the raw material from which corals, mussels, sea urchins and many microscopic plankton build shells and skeletons of calcium carbonate. As carbonate becomes scarcer, the saturation state of the water falls, and when it drops below one, unprotected structures of calcium carbonate begin to dissolve. This threshold has already been crossed in some deep waters. Polar seas, where cold water holds more dissolved gas, are expected to reach it first at the surface, perhaps within a few decades.

C. Pteropods, small swimming snails, are often described as the canaries of the sea. In laboratory exposures to the conditions projected for the end of the century, their delicate shells develop pitting and become thinner. Surveys along one western coastline have found a high proportion of animals with dissolution damage in water that had upwelled from depth, where the chemistry is naturally more corrosive. Their importance lies in food webs, since pteropods are eaten by herring and young salmon. Yet the authors of the surveys caution that laboratory exposures are often abrupt, and that animals in the wild may be partly protected by the way they behave, so the damage may be less dramatic than the tanks suggest.

D. Shellfish hatcheries offer a vivid case study. In the early years of the century, the Marrow Bay hatchery, which supplies oyster larvae to farms across the region, suffered repeated mass die-offs. The cause was eventually traced to bursts of upwelling that pushed corrosive water into the hatchery's intake pipes. Larvae are the life stage most at risk, because they must build their first shell within hours and have almost no energy reserves with which to do so. The hatchery responded with continuous monitoring, by drawing water only when its chemistry was favourable and by buffering the supply with sodium carbonate. Output recovered. The episode shows that acidification threatens economies as well as ecosystems, but also that adaptation is sometimes within reach.

E. The effects are not confined to organisms with shells. Experiments in the first decade of research suggested that elevated carbon dioxide impairs the behaviour of fish, leading them, for example, to lose their innate aversion to the smell of predators. The proposed mechanism was that fish regulating their internal acid-base balance in more acidic water alter the function of receptors in the nervous system. Later, larger studies found smaller effects, or none, in several species, and the early results are now widely regarded as having overestimated the problem. The picture varies markedly between species and between laboratories, and the field has become more cautious about generalising from a single experiment.

F. There will also be winners. Photosynthesising organisms such as seagrasses and some algae may benefit from the extra dissolved carbon dioxide, and certain calcifiers tolerate surprisingly acidic water. But benefits to individual species do not guarantee a healthy ecosystem, and acidification never acts alone. Warming and falling oxygen levels accompany it, and the stresses can compound one another. Organisms in coastal waters already experience large daily swings in pH and may be more tolerant than open-ocean species, which have evolved in stable chemistry. Natural carbon dioxide seeps near volcanic vents function as outdoor experiments. Around them, coral diversity declines and reefs give way to seagrass and fleshy algae. But seeps are imperfect analogues, because animals can recolonise from neighbouring areas, and the chemistry at a seep fluctuates far more than it will in the open ocean.

G. The geological record offers a further comparison. About 56 million years ago, a massive release of carbon was accompanied by extinctions among deep-sea bottom-dwelling organisms and by the dissolution of carbonate sediments. But the rate of that release was probably around ten times slower than today's. Rate matters, because slow change gives the weathering of rocks time to supply alkalinity and neutralise the added acid, over tens of thousands of years. Current emissions are outpacing any such buffer. Only cutting emissions addresses the cause. Local measures, such as restoring seagrass beds that draw down carbon dioxide or adding alkaline minerals to coastal waters, can reduce the harm in a particular bay, but none has yet been shown to work at the scale of an ocean.

items.text:
A. A globe is a faithful model of the Earth, but it is awkward to fold into a pocket or to print in an atlas, and so for centuries mapmakers have needed a systematic rule for transferring points from a sphere to a flat sheet. Such a rule is called a projection. In 1827, the mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss proved in his Theorema Egregium that no such transfer can preserve every geometric property. A curved surface cannot be flattened without stretching, shearing or tearing it, much as an orange peel cannot be laid flat without splitting. Every flat map is therefore a compromise, and the choice of a projection is in effect a choice about which distortions to tolerate.

B. The problem was understood in practice long before it was proved. Ptolemy, writing in the second century of the common era, described how the inhabited world might be drawn on a plane, using parallels of latitude drawn as arcs of circles so that the curvature of the Earth was suggested rather than ignored. When his text reached scholars in Western Europe in the early fifteenth century, it set a standard that mapmakers imitated for generations. Yet Ptolemy's methods were designed for a world that stretched only from the Atlantic to East Asia, and they proved increasingly strained as voyages revealed more of the globe.

C. The best-known solution to a particular problem was published in 1569 by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator. On his world map the meridians are parallel vertical lines, and the spacing between parallels increases steadily towards the poles. This spacing is calculated precisely so that angles are preserved locally, which makes the projection conformal. The result has a practical virtue that outweighed all its faults for navigators: a line of constant compass bearing, known as a rhumb line, appears as a straight line. A pilot could plot a course with a ruler and a protractor and follow it without continually adjusting the heading. The price is a steady inflation of area with distance from the equator. Greenland appears as large as Africa on such a map, although Africa is about fourteen times larger, and the poles cannot be shown at all, since they would lie infinitely far away.

D. In the eighteenth century, governments began to commission systematic surveys of their territories, and the demand for projections suited to particular regions grew. Johann Lambert, in a treatise of 1772, described several of the most useful, including conformal and equal-area designs. An equal-area projection preserves the relative size of regions, which is vital for maps of population, land use or soils, but it does so at the expense of shape. National mapping agencies learned to match the projection to the country. A conic projection, with its lines of equal distortion running east to west, suited a country extending broadly east to west in the middle latitudes, while a country elongated north to south required a different treatment. The era taught cartographers that no projection was best in the abstract, only best for a purpose.

E. The twentieth century produced compromise projections, designed to avoid extreme distortion of any one property instead of eliminating a single kind. The Winkel tripel, devised in 1921, averaged coordinates from three simpler constructions and kept distortions of area, angle and distance modest across the whole map. A leading geographical society adopted it for its world maps in 1998. Its predecessor in that role was a projection drawn up in 1963 by a mapmaker who selected its coordinates not by deriving them from a single formula but by adjusting tables of values until the world looked right to the eye. The approach shocked some mathematicians, but it acknowledged that a map is ultimately an image to be read by people, and that appearance counts for something.

F. In the 1970s, a campaign argued that the dominance of the Mercator projection in classrooms and offices gave schoolchildren a false impression of the relative importance of continents, and it promoted an equal-area alternative as a corrective. Most professional cartographers agreed that Mercator's projection was unsuitable for general world maps, a view that had been expressed years earlier, but they objected that the alternative, which stretches the tropics vertically, was hardly more faithful to the shapes of countries. The sharpest disagreement concerned a further claim, that wall maps shape the beliefs of those who look at them. The evidence for this is largely anecdotal, and the few studies that exist have produced mixed results, so the question remains open.

G. The shift to digital mapping has changed the debate rather than ended it. In 2005, the best-known online map services adopted a variant of the Mercator projection, commonly called web Mercator. At the scale of a street or a neighbourhood, preserving angles means that the shape of a junction on the screen matches its shape on the ground, and the mathematics of the projection makes it easy to divide the map into a pyramid of square tiles for fast loading. The variant applies spherical formulas to coordinates measured on an ellipsoid, which introduces small positional discrepancies that irritate surveyors. As users zoom out far enough to see whole continents, many services now switch to a globe view, which restores what the flat page cannot: the Earth's true shape. The lesson of five centuries of cartography is that a projection is a tool, and the right choice depends on the task.

items.text:
The table shows the percentage of adults in five countries who visited at least one museum in 2005 and in 2020, together with the average number of museum visits made per visitor in 2020.
Country: 2005 / 2020 / visits per visitor in 2020
Brevin: 56% / 49% / 4.2
Norland: 41% / 52% / 3.1
Estavia: 33% / 29% / 2.4
Kelmar: 18% / 31% / 1.9
Tolsen: 12% / 14% / 1.5
items.q: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
items.sample:
The table compares the proportion of adults who visited a museum in five countries in 2005 and 2020, and also gives the average number of visits per visitor in 2020. Overall, museum attendance rose in three of the five countries, and the countries with the highest attendance also tended to have the most frequent visitors.

Brevin had the highest attendance in 2005, at 56 percent, but its figure fell to 49 percent by 2020, which allowed Norland to overtake it. Norland's share of adults rose from 41 to 52 percent, the second largest increase in the table. The biggest rise occurred in Kelmar, where attendance climbed from 18 to 31 percent, an increase of 13 points. Tolsen changed very little, moving from 12 to 14 percent, and it remained the lowest-ranked country in both years. Estavia was the only other country to record a decline, from 33 to 29 percent.

Turning to the frequency of visits in 2020, Brevin's visitors went most often, with an average of 4.2 visits each, followed by those in Norland with 3.1. Visitors in Estavia made 2.4 visits, whereas Kelmar and Tolsen recorded only 1.9 and 1.5 respectively. It is notable that Kelmar's rapid growth in attendance has not yet been matched by a high frequency of visits, suggesting that many of its new visitors go only occasionally.

items.q: Some people think that governments should spend public money on space exploration. Others believe that this money should be used to solve problems on Earth. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
items.sample:
Few topics divide opinion as sharply as public spending on space exploration. Some people argue that the money would be better used to tackle hunger, disease and poverty at home, while others maintain that the benefits of exploring space justify the investment. In my view, both positions have merit, but a modest, sustained programme is easier to defend than either extreme.

Critics of space spending make an understandable point. Governments face competing demands, and a single launch can cost as much as a hospital or a network of rural schools. When millions of people lack clean water or basic healthcare, it can seem irresponsible to fund rockets and telescopes. There is also the argument that private companies are now willing to finance missions, so public money is no longer essential.

However, supporters of space programmes can point to benefits that are less obvious than the pictures of distant planets. Satellite technology underpins weather forecasting, navigation and communications, and it helps scientists monitor the climate and warn of disasters such as floods. Many materials and medical devices were first developed to meet the demands of spaceflight. Moreover, ambitious projects inspire young people to study science and engineering, which strengthens a country's economy in the long term. Private firms, for their part, tend to pursue only those projects that promise a quick profit, and they rarely fund the basic research from which later discoveries emerge.

It is also misleading to treat the choice as a simple trade between rockets and hospitals. Space agencies receive a small fraction of most national budgets, so cancelling them would release far less money than critics suppose, and it would not automatically be spent on the poor. The real question is one of balance rather than of principle.

In conclusion, governments should continue to support space exploration, but at a level that does not undermine essential services, and they should insist that the research serves practical goals as well as national prestige.

parts.instr: Part 2: Individual long turn.

items.q: Describe a skill that you taught yourself. You should say: what the skill is, how you learned it, what difficulties you had, and explain why it is useful to you.
items.sample: I would like to talk about the skill of repairing bicycles, which I taught myself about three years ago. It began when my own bicycle broke down on a long ride and I could not afford to pay a mechanic. I decided to try to fix it, and I started by watching videos and reading a manual that I borrowed from the library. I also practised on an old bicycle that my uncle gave me, which was useful because I could not do any real damage. The most difficult part was adjusting the gears, since the tiny screws have to be set exactly, and I made many mistakes before I understood how the system worked. Eventually, I could replace tyres, brakes and chains without any help. This skill is useful to me in several ways. First, it saves me money, because I no longer pay for simple repairs. Second, it gives me confidence, and I now help friends who have problems with their bicycles. I think I learned that patience matters more than talent.
items.vi: Part 2: mô tả một kỹ năng tự học, đủ bốn ý gợi ý (kỹ năng, cách học, khó khăn, lợi ích).

items.q: Why do some people find it easier to learn new skills than others?
items.sample: I think it depends on several factors. Some people are more motivated, and motivation makes them practise for longer. Others had good teachers when they were young, so they learned how to learn. Of course, natural ability plays a part, but I believe regular practice and a positive attitude matter more, because anyone who keeps trying will improve.
items.vi: Part 3: bàn về lý do khác biệt khi học kỹ năng, nêu nhiều yếu tố.

items.q: Should schools teach practical skills, such as repairing things, as well as academic subjects?
items.sample: In my opinion, schools should teach practical skills because many students will need them in daily life, whatever job they choose. Learning to repair simple things also develops problem solving and patience. However, schools have limited time, so practical lessons should complement academic subjects rather than replace them.
items.vi: Part 3: đưa quan điểm về dạy kỹ năng thực hành trong trường.

items.q: How might technology change the way adults learn in the future?
items.sample: I expect technology will make learning more flexible and personal in the future. Adults will be able to study short courses on their phones while they travel, and artificial tutors will adapt exercises to each learner. On the other hand, people may miss the motivation that comes from studying with others, so a mixture of online and face to face learning will probably be best.
items.vi: Part 3: dự đoán về công nghệ và việc học của người lớn, có cân nhắc hai mặt.

Yes, there are a few places left. Can I take your surname first?
It's Lonsdale. That's L-O-N-S-D-A-L-E.

parts.instr: Listen to a talk about a community orchard project and choose the correct answers.
parts.instrVi: Nghe bài nói về một dự án vườn cây ăn quả cộng đồng và chọn đáp án đúng.

audio.t: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming to this information evening about the Ashby Vale orchard project. I'm Rosalind Teague, the coordinator. I'll explain the background, what has been planted so far, and where we need your help.

The land belongs to the parish council. For decades it was a rough field used for car parking during the summer fair, and when the fair moved to the school grounds, it was simply abandoned. Several residents wanted to turn it into allotments, but a survey showed that the soil was too shallow and stony for vegetables. Fruit trees were suggested instead, as they have deeper roots and need less preparation.

We planted the first sixty trees last November, mainly apples, with a few pears and plums. We hope to reach one hundred by the end of next year. We deliberately chose older local varieties, some of which are no longer sold in supermarkets, because they tend to be more resistant to the diseases found in this valley. Taste was a secondary consideration, though the early signs are promising.

Funding came from three sources. A national charity paid for the trees, local businesses sponsored the fencing, and a crowdfunding appeal raised enough for tools and a storage shed. We did apply to the parish council for a grant but were turned down, which in hindsight made us more independent.

Rabbits were our biggest problem in the first winter. The fencing helped, but they got through underneath it in two places, so we've now buried wire mesh along the base. Deer haven't come yet, but a neighbour who knows about these things has warned us that it is only a matter of time.

Now, the volunteers. We have a core group of about twelve who come every Sunday morning, and some of them are very experienced at pruning. What we really need is people who can come on a weekday, since a lot of the watering and maintenance is best done then, and the Sunday group is rather stretched.

In the autumn we plan an apple day, when residents will bring fruit from their own gardens to be identified by an expert and pressed into juice. Last year's trial run was held in a small hall, and so many people came that we ran out of bottles, so this time we have booked the village hall.

There's also an education side. Two local primary schools have agreed to adopt a tree each, and the children will visit every season to record blossom dates and measure growth. The teachers see it as a way of linking science lessons to real observation.

If you'd like to help, there's a sign-up sheet at the back, and I'll stay behind for questions. Please note that we can't accept donations of mature trees, however kind the offer, as we need to keep the collection consistent. Thank you.

parts.instr: Listen to two students talking to their tutor about a research project and choose the correct answers.
parts.instrVi: Nghe hai sinh viên trao đổi với gia sư về một dự án nghiên cứu và chọn đáp án đúng.

audio.t: Come in. So, you've chosen to look at school start times for your sociology project. Tell me where you've got to.

We've read a good deal about adolescent sleep. The biological argument seems strong, because teenagers' body clocks shift later, so asking them to be alert at eight is like asking an adult to start work at five.
Though I'm not sure that's the whole story. Some of the studies we found confused sleep with other changes, like schools introducing breakfast clubs at the same time as a later start.
That's a fair point, and it's worth stating in your methodology. The strongest studies compare similar schools where only the start time differs. What are you planning yourselves?
We'd like to survey students at the three schools in the district. One of them moved its start time from a quarter past eight to nine o'clock two years ago.
That's a useful natural experiment. But beware of memory. If you ask students how well they slept two years ago, the answers will be unreliable.
So we should only ask about the present and compare across the schools?
Yes, and I'd add attendance records, which don't depend on memory. Ask the schools for their lateness figures as well as the absence figures.
We were worried that the head teachers would refuse.
Some may, but present it as helping them, because the schools gain from the evidence. Send a short letter rather than an email, which is easy to ignore, and offer to share your findings.
Should we worry about sample size? Each school has about six hundred students, and we can't survey all of them.

Around eighty per school would be adequate, provided the sample is random. Forty would be too thin to compare, and a hundred and twenty is more than you can analyse in the time. And don't just ask your friends.
We'd planned to hand out questionnaires in assembly. Is that all right?
I'd avoid that. Students feel pressure in a hall full of their classmates and may answer the way they think they ought to. Better to give them an online form that they complete privately.
Right. The other thing we weren't sure about was the literature review. How many sources do we need?
Quality over quantity. About fifteen well-chosen articles, but make sure that some of them argue against your hypothesis.
We found one paper claiming that later start times simply push everything later, so that students stay up later still.
That's exactly the kind of counter-evidence I mean. Discuss it properly, and say what would be needed to settle the question.
When is the deadline for the first draft?
The twelfth of November, but I'd like to see your questionnaire before the end of this month so that I can comment on it.
And the final report?
Due in January. The word limit is four thousand, not five thousand as the old handbook says. It was revised last year.

items.q: What does the man say about some of the studies they read?
options: They ignored the biology of adolescent sleep.
They were based on very small samples.
They confused sleep with other changes introduced at the same time.
items.vi: Anh ấy nói một số nghiên cứu nhầm lẫn giấc ngủ với những thay đổi khác như câu lạc bộ ăn sáng.

items.q: What does the tutor think of the school that changed its start time?
options: It is too different from the other schools.
It provides a useful natural experiment.
It should be left out of the survey.
items.vi: Gia sư gọi đó là một thí nghiệm tự nhiên hữu ích.

items.q: What problem does the tutor see with asking about sleep two years ago?
options: Memories of the past are unreliable.
Students will not want to answer.
The questions would take too long.
items.vi: Hỏi về giấc ngủ hai năm trước sẽ cho câu trả lời không đáng tin vì phụ thuộc vào trí nhớ.

items.q: What additional source of data does the tutor suggest?
items.vi: Gia sư đề nghị hồ sơ đi học muộn và vắng mặt vì chúng không phụ thuộc vào trí nhớ.

items.q: What advice does the tutor give about approaching head teachers?
options: Ask the university to write on their behalf.
Send a letter and offer to share the findings.
items.vi: Gửi thư ngắn thay vì email và đề nghị chia sẻ kết quả.

items.q: How many students per school does the tutor recommend surveying?
items.vi: Khoảng 80 mỗi trường là đủ nếu mẫu ngẫu nhiên; 40 quá ít, 120 quá nhiều để phân tích.

audio.t: Good morning. Today I want to look at the acoustics of ancient theatres, and in particular at how the Greeks and Romans managed to make speech audible to thousands of people without any amplification.

First, the setting. The Greek theatre at Epidaurus, built in the fourth century BC, held around fourteen thousand spectators. Visitors today are often amazed that a coin dropped on the central stage can be heard in the very last row. The seating area is shaped like a shallow bowl, and the slope of the rows is about twenty-six degrees, which is steep enough for every spectator to see the performers clearly.

Now, why does the sound carry so well? For a long time, people credited the design of the stone seats. Researchers have shown that the rows of limestone seats act as a filter. They reduce low-frequency background noise, such as the murmur of the crowd, while allowing the higher frequencies of the human voice to reach the back. The effect is similar to a filter on a modern microphone, and it works best when the audience is seated, because people's bodies absorb some of the sound.

The second feature is the stage building, called the skene. Behind the actors stood a tall wall, which reflected the voices forward towards the audience. In Roman theatres the wall was often decorated with columns and statues, and it was usually built of stone rather than wood, because stone reflects sound more efficiently. Roman architects also added a roof over the stage in many cases, which helped to project the sound outwards.

The Roman writer Vitruvius described another idea. He recommended placing bronze vessels, tuned to different notes, under the seats, to resonate with the actors' voices. However, no such vessels have been found in the great majority of theatres, and modern tests suggest that they would have had little effect. So most scholars now regard his advice as theory rather than practice.

Actors also helped. They wore masks with open mouths, and some historians believe that these acted as small megaphones. More importantly, performers were trained to speak slowly and clearly, and the plays were written in verse, with a strong rhythm that made the words easier to follow at a distance.

Position mattered too. Theatres were usually built on hillsides, away from towns and roads, so there was little traffic noise. Wind could be a problem, however, and builders often chose a site sheltered from the prevailing wind. Even so, the audience in the highest rows of the biggest theatres probably missed some words.

Finally, a note on method. Researchers cannot simply test these theatres under original conditions, because the stone has weathered and many of the stage walls have been lost. So we use computer models, and small-scale replicas, to estimate what the audience once heard. For next week, please read the chapter on medieval cathedrals.

items.text:
A
For most of the twentieth century, the textbook account of heredity was admirably tidy. Genes, stretches of DNA, passed from parents to offspring, and whatever an individual experienced during its lifetime left no trace on that inheritance. A blacksmith's strong arms did not make his children strong, and the notion that acquired characteristics could be inherited, associated with the discredited ideas of Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, was treated by most biologists with a certain embarrassment. Yet a minority suspected that the story was incomplete. Every cell in a human body carries essentially the same DNA, but a neuron and a liver cell behave in profoundly different ways. Something other than the sequence itself must tell each cell which genes to read and which to ignore, and that something has to be stable enough to survive each time the cell divides.

B
The study of that something is now called epigenetics, a term coined by the embryologist Conrad Waddington in 1942. The best understood mechanisms are chemical tags attached either to the DNA or to the histone proteins around which it is wound. When methyl groups settle on particular stretches of DNA, the genes nearby tend to fall silent. When histones are modified in other ways, the same region may become more accessible and its genes more active. None of this changes the order of the chemical letters in the genome. The marks resemble annotations in the margin of a manuscript, instructions about which passages are to be performed and which left unread. Crucially, the annotations can be rewritten by the cell's surroundings, including diet, stress and exposure to toxins, which is why two genetically identical organisms can end up quite different.

C
Most of this annotation is erased twice in each generation: once in the cells that give rise to eggs and sperm, and again soon after fertilisation. The wipe is thought to give the embryo a clean slate from which it can become any kind of cell. It follows that any claim of epigenetic inheritance must show that certain marks escape the erasure. For years the best evidence was circumstantial. People who had been in the womb during the Dutch famine of 1944 to 1945 were found, decades later, to have an elevated incidence of metabolic disease and measurable differences in methylation at several genes. Yet such findings could not separate biological transmission from the consequences of upbringing, since the affected families shared hunger, poverty and, afterwards, similar eating habits. Nor, for the same reason, could they show whether the marks, or only the circumstances, had been handed on to the grandchildren.

D
Laboratory animals offer cleaner tests. A team led by Dr. Imara Lindqvist of the Norrby Institute fed male mice a diet low in protein for several weeks before mating them with females that had eaten normally. The pups never experienced their fathers' diet, and they never met their fathers either, because the males were removed after mating, which ruled out any effect of parental behaviour. Even so, the pups showed altered activity in liver genes involved in fat metabolism, although the fathers' DNA sequences were unchanged. Tracing the effect further, the team found that sperm from the underfed males carried a distinctive mixture of small RNA molecules, and injecting that mixture into normal embryos produced similar changes. The authors were careful to describe their result as a demonstration that a signal can cross a generation, not as proof that it persists beyond one.

E
Sceptics point out that such results are fragile. Prof. Tobias Ashgrove, a geneticist, accepts that inherited epigenetic effects are well documented in plants and have been reported in a roundworm, where a learned avoidance of a harmful bacterium persisted for several generations before fading. He argues, however, that the evidence in mammals is far thinner. Many findings, he notes, have not been reproduced, the effects are small by comparison with ordinary genetic variation, and apparent epigenetic differences between individuals may in fact be caused by subtle differences in their DNA sequences, which would make the epigenetic explanation redundant. He is also dismayed by popular accounts claiming that trauma is inherited through the genome, describing them as a leap from suggestive rodent data to human destiny that the evidence does not support.

F
Whatever the final verdict on transgenerational effects, the field's practical importance lies elsewhere. Epigenetic marks change in a predictable way as people age, which has allowed researchers to construct 'clocks' that estimate biological age from a blood sample. Drugs that remove methyl groups from DNA are already used to treat certain blood cancers, on the principle that tumour cells silence protective genes by methylation. And the epigenetic perspective has altered the old argument between nature and nurture, which assumed that the two operate separately. If the environment can write instructions that the genome then obeys, the boundary between them is not a wall but a membrane. Where the debate over inheritance has moved is from whether such effects exist to how often they occur, how long they last, and how much they matter.

items.text:
A
In 1971 the economist and psychologist Herbert Simon observed that a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention. At the time he was thinking of managers drowning in memoranda, but the remark has since aged into something close to a business plan. If information is cheap to produce and to copy, then what is scarce is the human capacity to notice it, and whatever is scarce commands a price. An economy has gradually grown up around the buying and selling of that capacity, and its central peculiarity is that the people being sold seldom see an invoice. Nobody pays for a search engine, a video platform or a news site with money. They pay with minutes, and the minutes are resold to advertisers at a rate that, for the largest firms, amounts to a fortune.

B
The logic of this arrangement is easier to see by comparison with older media. A newspaper in the nineteenth century sold copies to readers and, at the same time, sold the readers' glances to advertisers, but the paper's content had to be good enough to justify the purchase price. Once the price falls to zero, that discipline weakens. The platform's revenue depends not on how satisfied its users are but on how long they stay and how often they return, and the two can diverge. A product that leaves its customers slightly dissatisfied and unable to stop may earn more than one that leaves them contented and ready to leave. Economists describe this as a gap between what users choose and what they would choose on reflection, a gap that conventional market theory, which treats choice as revealing preference, is poorly equipped to handle.

C
Measuring the gap is difficult, because the price needed for the usual calculation does not exist. One ingenious approach was taken by Dr. Renata Oyelaran, who recruited about two thousand regular users of a video service and offered half of them money to stop using it for a month. She also asked everyone beforehand how much they would need to be paid to give it up. The stated figures were high, yet the participants who actually switched off reported, afterwards, modest gains in wellbeing and spent more time with friends and on hobbies. Strikingly, a month later, many of them had returned to nearly the same level of use as before. Oyelaran's reading is cautious. The users plainly valued the service, but their valuation seemed partly to reflect habit and the fear of missing out, which depends on everyone else being present.

D
Habit matters because attention, unlike money, cannot be saved. An hour not spent on one thing is simply gone, and rival sellers know that every minute they win is a minute taken from someone else. This turns the market into something like an arms race. When one firm introduces a feature, such as an endless scroll or a notification that arrives at the moment a user is most likely to respond, its competitors must copy it or lose ground, and yet the total quantity of attention available stays fixed. All the firms spend more, and the sum of their revenues is no greater. The costs fall on a third party, the user, whose time and concentration are spent in ways that no one has asked him or her to approve. Some economists therefore treat attention as a kind of commons, a shared resource vulnerable to being overgrazed.

E
Not everyone accepts the picture of a fixed stock. Prof. Lucan Hesse argues that attention is more elastic than the metaphor suggests, because people routinely combine activities, listening to a podcast while cooking or watching a match with a second screen in hand. Total media consumption has grown, he points out, and advertisements are not always a nuisance, since they can inform consumers of products they would actually want to buy. Psychologists, however, caution that what looks like multitasking is usually rapid switching, and that each switch carries a cost in accuracy and recall. The expansion Hesse describes is therefore real in terms of hours but may be shallower in terms of what is absorbed, which complicates any attempt to count attention as if every minute were equal.

F
Policy proposals reflect these disagreements. Some would tax revenue from highly targeted advertising, on the grounds that it rewards the most effective capture of attention. Others favour changing the defaults, so that autoplay and infinite scrolling are switched off unless a user chooses otherwise, a modest intervention with a large effect if most people never change a setting. A third group distrusts regulation altogether and expects consumers to adapt, as they once adapted to junk mail and billboards. Whichever course is chosen, enforcement will be difficult, since regulators must define in law what counts as capturing attention rather than simply providing something people want. What unites the camps is the recognition that a resource previously taken for granted now has a market, and that its price, though never printed on a receipt, is real.

items.text:
A
Humans worked metal long before they smelted it. The earliest copper objects, from the Near East around nine thousand years ago, were hammered from native copper, nuggets found lying in the ground, and treated much like a soft stone. Smelting, the chemical reduction of ore by heat in an oxygen-poor atmosphere, arrived several millennia later and changed the situation entirely, because ore is far more abundant than native metal. Copper was still a poor material for tools, however. Pure copper is soft, and when it is cast it tends to fill with gas bubbles. Early smiths found that adding small quantities of arsenic, probably by smelting ores in which it occurred naturally, produced a harder and more castable metal, although at a cost to the health of the workers, whose fumes were poisonous.

B
The decisive step was the deliberate alloying of copper with tin, which yields bronze. With roughly one part of tin to nine of copper, the alloy is considerably harder than copper, melts at a lower temperature, and flows more readily into a mould. It also keeps its edge better and can be re-melted indefinitely. These advantages were bought at the price of dependence. Copper ores occur in many regions, but tin is rare, and the major deposits lay far from the centres that wanted it. Bronze-making societies in Mesopotamia, for example, relied on tin that had to travel across mountains and deserts from sources in what is now Central Asia, while the tin of Atlantic Europe came largely from the south-west of Britain. The result was one of the first long-distance trading systems of which archaeologists can trace the outlines.

C
Casting technology advanced alongside alloy chemistry. Open stone moulds produced flat axes and simple blades, but hollow objects such as socketed spearheads required closed two-piece moulds, and for complex forms smiths used the lost-wax method. A model was shaped in beeswax, covered in clay and fired. The wax ran out, leaving a cavity into which molten bronze was poured, and the clay was then broken away, so that each cast was unique, a quality that suits both sculpture and ceremonial objects. Evidence of skill is not confined to casting. Finished pieces were hammered, annealed to restore their ductility, and polished or decorated, and microscopic examination shows that some smiths deliberately worked the edge of a blade to harden it. Such details suggest that the craft was learned through long apprenticeship rather than discovered by accident.

D
Much of what is now known about the trade networks derives from chemistry rather than from texts. Lead isotope analysis exploits the fact that ores from different deposits carry different ratios of isotopes, and that those ratios survive smelting. Dr. Pellam Ostrander's team applied the technique to more than four hundred objects from the Karrowdun hoard, a cache buried beside a river crossing around 1300 BCE. To their surprise, the copper came from at least five distinct regions, some more than a thousand kilometres away, and objects that looked alike often came from different sources. Ostrander concluded that the smiths of Karrowdun were not tied to a single supplier but bought metal, much of it in the form of ingots, wherever it was available, and that style travelled more easily than material.

E
Who controlled this trade is debated. A traditional view holds that rulers monopolised bronze, using it to arm their followers and to display wealth, and that the metal therefore explains the emergence of a warrior elite. Prof. Marit Solheim has challenged this, pointing out that excavated workshops are frequently found in ordinary settlements, that bronze scrap was widely circulated, and that hoards of broken objects, long assumed to be offerings, may instead be the stock of itinerant smiths who recycled old metal into new. If she is right, bronze working was less a palace industry than a network of craftspeople, whose mobility helps explain how technical knowledge spread so quickly. Her critics respond that the largest and most elaborate objects still cluster around the wealthiest burials, which suggests that some elite groups did at least consume the finest work.

F
The end of the Bronze Age, in the eastern Mediterranean around 1200 BCE, is often linked to the rise of iron, but the connection is not what one might expect. Early iron was not better than bronze. Smelted iron required higher temperatures than ancient furnaces could easily reach, produced a spongy mass that had to be hammered, and, until smiths learned to introduce carbon through prolonged heating in charcoal, yielded a metal no harder than good bronze. What iron offered was availability. Its ores are found almost everywhere, and when disruption of the long-distance trade cut off the supply of tin, communities turned to a material they could find locally. Only later, as techniques improved, did iron become the superior metal. The change thus owed more to supply than to superiority, a pattern that technological history repeats more often than its popular accounts admit.

items.text:
The table shows the percentage of electricity generated from four sources in three countries in 1995 and in 2020.

Norvale 1995: coal 62, gas 12, nuclear 20, renewables 6
Norvale 2020: coal 18, gas 31, nuclear 22, renewables 29
Delmar 1995: coal 28, gas 35, nuclear 30, renewables 7
Delmar 2020: coal 5, gas 40, nuclear 27, renewables 28
Karsten 1995: coal 85, gas 5, nuclear 0, renewables 10
Karsten 2020: coal 61, gas 14, nuclear 0, renewables 25

Note: figures are percentages of total electricity generation.
items.q: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
items.sample:
The table compares the share of electricity produced from coal, gas, nuclear power and renewable sources in three countries in 1995 and 2020. Overall, coal declined in every country while renewables grew substantially, although the pace of change differed considerably.

In 1995 coal dominated in Karsten, at 85 percent, and in Norvale, at 62 percent, whereas Delmar relied mainly on gas and nuclear power, at 35 and 30 percent. By 2020, coal had fallen to just 5 percent in Delmar and 18 percent in Norvale. Karsten reduced its dependence by a smaller margin, from 85 to 61 percent, so coal remained its principal source.

Renewables showed the most striking increase. Their share in Norvale rose from 6 to 29 percent, and in Delmar from 7 to 28 percent, while Karsten's figure climbed from 10 to 25 percent. Gas also expanded in all three countries, most notably in Norvale, where it rose from 12 to 31 percent. Nuclear power stayed relatively stable in Norvale and Delmar, and Karsten did not use it at either date.

items.q: Some people believe that automation will reduce the number of jobs available, while others think it will create new kinds of work. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
items.sample:
Advances in robotics and software have led many people to fear that machines will take over the work of human beings. Others argue that technology has always generated new occupations. In this essay I will examine both views before explaining why I find the second more convincing, provided that governments respond sensibly.

Those who expect job losses can point to clear evidence. Automation has already replaced many workers in factories, warehouses and ticket offices, and software is now capable of tasks such as translating documents or screening medical images, which were once thought to require human judgement. Because machines do not need wages or rest, employers have a strong financial reason to adopt them, and the people affected are often those with the least education and the fewest alternatives.

On the other hand, history suggests that technological change creates as many jobs as it destroys. When mechanised looms and later computers appeared, entire industries vanished, yet new ones emerged that nobody had predicted, from software development to online retail. Cheaper production also lowers prices, which gives consumers more money to spend on other goods and services, and that spending supports employment elsewhere. In addition, many jobs consist of a mixture of tasks, and automation tends to remove the routine ones while leaving the human elements of care, creativity and persuasion.

In my opinion, the second view is closer to the truth, but it should not be a reason for complacency. The new jobs rarely appear in the same places, or for the same people, as the old ones. Workers displaced in one town cannot easily take up a technical position in another. Governments should therefore invest in retraining and in education that develops flexible skills, and they should support those who face a long period without work.

In conclusion, automation will change the kind of jobs available rather than simply reduce their number, but the benefits will only be shared fairly if society prepares for the transition.

items.q: Is there a place in your town where you like to spend time?
items.sample: Yes, there is a quiet park near the river in my town where I like to spend time. I often go there at weekends to relax, read a book or just watch people passing by. It is a good place to forget about work.
items.vi: Nói về một địa điểm yêu thích trong thị trấn.

parts.instr: Part 2: Talk about the topic on the card for one to two minutes.
parts.instrVi: Phần 2: nói về chủ đề trên thẻ trong một đến hai phút.

items.q: Describe a place you would like to visit again. You should say: where the place is, when you went there, what you did there, and explain why you would like to go back.
items.sample: I would like to talk about Kyoto, in Japan, which I would love to visit again. I went there about four years ago with two close friends, during the spring holiday. We stayed in a small guesthouse near the old town and spent five days walking between temples, gardens and traditional markets. I especially remember an early morning visit to a bamboo forest, when there were hardly any other tourists, and the light through the trees was beautiful. We also tried a tea ceremony and tasted many local dishes. I would like to go back for several reasons. First, we were so busy that we missed many places, including some mountain temples. Second, I would like to see the city in autumn, when the leaves change colour. Finally, the calm atmosphere helped me relax, and I think I would appreciate it even more now.
items.vi: Part 2: mô tả một nơi muốn quay lại thăm, đủ bốn ý (ở đâu, khi nào, làm gì, vì sao muốn quay lại).

parts.instr: Part 3: Discuss more abstract questions related to the Part 2 topic.
parts.instrVi: Phần 3: thảo luận các câu hỏi trừu tượng liên quan đến chủ đề phần 2.

items.q: Why do some people prefer to visit the same place many times rather than new places?
items.sample: I think some people feel comfortable in familiar places, because they know what to expect and do not need to plan much. It is also relaxing, since they can enjoy the holiday without stress. Others build friendships or memories in a place, so returning feels like going home.
items.vi: Giải thích vì sao có người thích quay lại cùng một nơi.

items.q: How has tourism changed the places that people like to visit?
items.sample: Tourism has brought money and jobs to many places, but it has also made popular sites very crowded. Prices often rise, and local people sometimes lose their traditional way of life. However, with good management, tourism can help to protect heritage and the environment.
items.vi: Tác động của du lịch lên các địa điểm, có cả mặt tích cực và tiêu cực.

items.q: Do you think travelling to other countries is better than exploring your own country?
items.sample: I think both have value. Travelling abroad lets people experience different cultures and languages, which broadens the mind. However, many people have not seen the beautiful places in their own country, and domestic trips are usually cheaper and better for the environment.
items.vi: So sánh du lịch nước ngoài và trong nước, có cân nhắc hai phía.

audio.t: Good morning, Harbourside Sailing Academy. How can I help?
Hello. I would like to book a place on your beginners' dinghy course, please. I saw an advertisement at the library.
Certainly. That is the Weekend Dinghy Skills course. Could I take your surname first?
It's Thackeray. That's T-H-A-C-K-E-R-A-Y.
Thank you, Mr Thackeray. And your postcode, so that I can send you the joining pack?
HR4 7QL.
HR4 7QL. Lovely. Now, I should say that the course runs on Saturday mornings, not Sundays. We used to offer Sundays, but the harbour gets too busy.
Saturday is fine. When does the next course begin?
The brochure says the twenty-first of September, but we have had to move it back a week because of building work at the slipway, so it will now begin on the twenty-eighth.
Right. And how much is it?
The fee is one hundred and eighty-five pounds for the six sessions. It was a hundred and sixty last year, but our insurance costs have risen.
That seems reasonable. Do I need to bring anything?

Wear clothes you don't mind getting wet. A lot of beginners buy waterproof trousers as well, but they aren't necessary at this stage. The waterproof jacket is the one thing you must have. We provide life jackets and boots.
And where do we meet? At the main car park?
No, at the boathouse office, which is next to the fuel pontoon. The car park is a bit of a walk away.
Have you done any sailing before, Mr Thackeray?
Only once, on a lake, in a friend's boat, years ago. I certainly wouldn't call myself experienced.
That's perfectly all right. One more thing. We don't provide lunch, but you can bring your own, and there is a kitchen in the clubhouse where you can heat it up.
Good to know. How do I secure my place?
We need a deposit within seven days. We can hold the place for ten days at the most, but if the deposit hasn't reached us within a week we start to contact the waiting list.
I'll pay it this afternoon, then. Thank you very much.

parts.instr: Listen to a guide talking to visitors and choose the correct answer.
parts.instrVi: Nghe hướng dẫn viên nói chuyện với du khách và chọn đáp án đúng.

audio.t: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Pennant Bridge Tramway Museum. Before we set off, let me explain how the day will work.

The museum is forty years old this year. It began when a group of retired engineers rescued three tramcars from a scrapyard. Their original aim was modest: they only wanted to restore a single car as a memorial to the old line. They did not intend to start a museum, and certainly not to reopen any track, but donations arrived so quickly that the project grew far beyond that.

Many visitors assume that the line closed in 1953 because of competition from buses. In fact, buses were a minor factor. The real cause was the decline of the shipyard that the trams served; once the yard shrank, there were simply not enough passengers, and a fire at the depot in 1951 only made matters worse.

Today, the heritage line has three stops, and trams run every twenty minutes. The ride from end to end takes about fifteen minutes. Your ticket is valid all day, and you may get on and off as often as you like, so please don't feel that you have to stay on board for the whole journey.

Our oldest vehicle, car number nine, was built in 1902. You won't find it in the main collection hall at the moment, because it is being repainted. However, you can watch the work through the glass viewing window in the workshop, which is next to the first stop.

Almost everyone who works here is a volunteer. You might think that drivers are the hardest people to recruit, but we train those ourselves. What we struggle to find are skilled upholsterers, because the original seats were stuffed with horsehair and covered in leather, and very few people still know the techniques. Carpenters and electricians are also welcome, though we do have enough of them for now.

A word about refreshments. The cafe by the main entrance is closed for refurbishment until next spring. In the meantime, there is a temporary kiosk beside the second stop, which sells hot drinks and sandwiches. There is no need to carry food with you, but picnics are allowed on the lawn.

Photography is encouraged throughout the museum, with one exception. Please don't take photographs in the signal box simulator, because the screens are light-sensitive and flashes distort the display. Tripods are fine in the collection hall as long as they do not block the walkways.

For younger visitors, we have a driving simulator. You must be at least ten years old to use it, although smaller children can ring the bell on the real tram with a member of staff. Please ask at the second stop.

If you enjoy today, do come back for our night tram event. It is held on the last Friday of every month, not the first, as some of our older leaflets say, and the cars are decorated with lamps. Finally, the shop: all profits go towards extending the track as far as the river, which is our dream for the next decade. Enjoy your visit.

audio.t: Come in, both of you. Let's go through your project proposal. You're looking at rooftop beehives, I believe.

That's right, Dr Lindqvist. We want to find out whether the hives affect wild bees. The number of hives in the city has risen sharply in the last ten years, but hardly anyone has studied what that does to the wild species.
I have to admit that I only got interested when Marta's neighbour put hives on her roof. Before that, I assumed keeping bees was automatically good for the environment.

Many people do. The honeybee is a managed animal, not a wild one, so it is a fair question. Now, you plan to compare twelve sites. That is a small sample, but it is acceptable if you pair each hive site with a site of similar size and similar planting.
We thought about using a lot more sites, but we couldn't get permission for more rooftops.
Which brings me to counting. How do you plan to record the bees?
We were going to do timed walks along a fixed route and count every bee we see on the flowers.

I would be cautious. The results depend heavily on the observer's eyesight and experience. Coloured pan traps, which are shallow bowls of soapy water, are less biased, although I appreciate that some people dislike the fact that the insects are killed. If you do use traps, keep them to the minimum number that gives usable data.
We would rather avoid killing them, so perhaps we could use the walks but have both of us count independently.

That would be a reasonable compromise, and you can then check how closely your numbers agree. Whichever method you choose, only survey on dry days when the temperature is above fifteen degrees, otherwise the counts will be too low and meaningless.
What about identification? We can't tell most wild bees apart by sight.
Nobody expects species names from photographs. Group them into types, such as bumblebees, mining bees and so on, and describe them as morphospecies. Just be clear in your report about what you did.
One thing worries us. Some of the green spaces are much bigger than others, and big parks naturally have more bees.

Exactly, so you must control for that. Record the area of each site and include it in the analysis. As for statistics, Kofi, you mentioned an average comparison. Because your sites are paired, a paired test is more suitable than comparing the group averages.
Right. We will also need to contact the building managers. Should we start with them?
I would contact the local beekeepers' association first. They know which roofs have hives and they can introduce you to the managers, which saves a lot of time.
And the timetable? We were thinking of fieldwork in June and July.
That should coincide with the peak of flowering. Aim to finish all the counts by the end of July, because the draft is due in September.
Is there anything we should be careful about when we write it up?

Yes. Your design can only show correlation, not cause. If you find fewer wild bees near hives, you cannot say that the hives are responsible, so present your limitations honestly. A modest, well-argued conclusion will score higher than a bold one.

audio.t: Today I want to talk about how scientists monitor active volcanoes. There are around fifteen hundred potentially active volcanoes on Earth, and the aim of monitoring is to detect the warning signs of an eruption early enough for people to be evacuated.

The most important method is seismology. Before an eruption, magma moves upwards through the rock and breaks it, which produces many small earthquakes. Scientists place instruments called seismometers on the flanks of a volcano, and a sudden increase in the number of tremors is usually the earliest warning sign.

The second method is measuring ground deformation. As magma accumulates underground, the surface of the volcano swells like a balloon. Tiltmeters can detect changes of a few millionths of a degree, and satellites using radar can measure movements of just a few millimetres across a whole mountain.

Third, we study the gases that escape from the volcano. Rising magma releases sulphur dioxide, and scientists measure how much is released each day, either by flying instruments through the plume or by using special cameras on the ground. When the amount of sulphur dioxide rises sharply, it suggests that fresh magma is close to the surface.

A fourth technique is thermal imaging. Satellites and drones carry cameras that record heat, so that a crater which is getting hotter, or a new lake of lava, can be seen even when the summit is hidden by cloud.

Of course, monitoring has limits. Every volcano behaves differently, and some give warnings only a few hours before an eruption. For that reason, scientists combine several types of data, rather than relying on one signal.

Now I'd like to mention an example. On Mount Pinatubo, in the Philippines, scientists noticed rising seismic activity and gas emissions in 1991. Because of their warnings, about sixty thousand people were evacuated before the huge eruption, and many thousands of lives were saved.

Finally, the future. Researchers are testing sensors that listen to very low sounds called infrasound, which can reveal explosions many kilometres away, and they are using computer models and artificial intelligence to compare patterns with past eruptions, so that forecasts will become more accurate.
