items.text:
A. For most of recorded history, the loss of consciousness was treated as a curiosity of sleep and sickness rather than as a scientific instrument. That changed in the middle of the nineteenth century, when surgeons discovered that certain vapours could abolish the experience of pain without abolishing the patient. Yet a puzzle at the heart of the discovery has persisted. Anaesthetists can reliably switch awareness off and on, hundreds of thousands of times a day, and still nobody can say with confidence what it is that they are switching. Dr Imogen Halvarsen, a neuroscientist who has studied the problem for three decades, calls anaesthesia "the only experiment in consciousness that is performed routinely, on a vast scale, and with a reliable reversal".

B. The chemistry is, paradoxically, both well understood and baffling. Molecules as different as xenon, a noble gas that barely reacts with anything, and propofol, a large oily compound, produce much the same behavioural result. This diversity troubled researchers for a century, because it suggested that there was no single receptor to which anaesthetics bound. Early in the twentieth century, a correlation between an agent's solubility in oil and its potency led to the theory that the drugs dissolve in the fatty membranes of neurons and disturb them in general. That idea has since been refined rather than abandoned. Most modern agents are now known to act on specific proteins embedded in the membrane, notably those that dampen neuronal firing, but the proteins vary from one drug to another, and none of them accounts for the whole effect.

C. Attention has therefore shifted from molecules to networks. In a series of experiments at the Tenbrook Institute, volunteers were given propofol in carefully increasing doses while an array of electrodes recorded their brain activity. As the dose rose, the volunteers stopped responding to spoken commands, but their brains did not fall silent. Neurons continued to fire, and sensory areas continued to register sounds. What changed was the way in which different regions communicated with one another. A pulse of magnetic stimulation delivered to the cortex of a waking person produces a long, complex pattern of echoes that travels across many areas; delivered under anaesthesia, the same pulse produces a brief local ripple that quickly dies away. The researchers concluded that consciousness depends less on how active the brain is than on how richly its parts can influence one another.

D. This interpretation, sometimes called the integration view, has an appealing consequence: it offers a measurable index. A "perturbation complexity" score derived from the echo pattern separates waking from deep anaesthesia with remarkable accuracy, and it has been applied to patients who seem unresponsive after brain injury, a few of whom have turned out to produce scores typical of wakefulness. Critics, however, point out that a measure which correlates with consciousness is not an explanation of it. The score might merely track a biological precondition, in the way that a healthy heartbeat is necessary for thought without being its source. Halvarsen concedes the point but argues that every mature science began with indicators before it arrived at theories; thermometers, she observes, preceded thermodynamics.

E. A further complication comes from what is termed "connected consciousness". In the isolated forearm technique, a tourniquet prevents the muscle-paralysing drug from reaching one arm, so that an anaesthetised patient can still squeeze a hand on request. In the Corvane trial, around one patient in twelve who appeared to be adequately anaesthetised did exactly that, yet almost none of them could remember anything afterwards. Were these patients conscious and simply unable to form memories, or were they responding without any experience at all? The data cannot decide the question, and the answer matters, because it determines whether an unresponsive patient can be assumed to be unaware.

F. Such findings complicate the clinical goal. Anaesthetists have traditionally aimed at unresponsiveness, but unresponsiveness is behavioural, whereas what matters ethically is experience. Accidental awareness occurs in perhaps one operation in several thousand, usually when doses are reduced for fragile patients. Monitors that translate electrical brain signals into a single number have reduced these events, though not eliminated them, partly because the algorithms were calibrated on one class of drug and perform less reliably with others. Ketamine, for example, produces a dissociated state in which patients may appear awake, with open eyes, while reporting vivid dreamlike experiences, and the standard monitors read such patients poorly.

G. Ketamine thus illustrates a broader lesson, which is that consciousness is not a single switch. Wakefulness, awareness of the environment and the sense of being a particular self can come apart, and different drugs dissect them in different ways. Halvarsen therefore argues that the question "when does consciousness vanish?" is badly posed, and that it would be more productive to ask what is lost first and what last. The evidence so far suggests that the sense of self fades before sensory responsiveness does, and returns after it. Whether that order reflects the architecture of the brain or merely the pharmacology of the drugs remains an open question, and a convincing theory will have to explain it.

items.text:
A. By most estimates, more than half of the world's workers earn their living in the informal economy: those activities, from street vending and domestic service to rickshaw driving, waste collection and home-based manufacturing, that operate largely outside regulation and taxation. When the term entered economic vocabulary in the early 1970s, planners took it for granted that such work was a transitional phenomenon, a waiting room through which rural migrants would pass on their way to formal employment as industrial economies matured. Half a century later, that expectation has not been borne out. In many cities, the informal sector has grown faster than the formal one, and in some it provides the majority of new jobs.

B. Three broad schools of thought have competed to explain this persistence. The dualists regard the informal sector as a residual category, a refuge for people whose skills are too limited to secure formal jobs; on this view, informality is a symptom of poverty and will fade as education improves. The structuralists reject the idea of two separate worlds. They argue that informal enterprises are woven into the formal economy, supplying it with cheap labour and inputs, and that large firms benefit from the arrangement by avoiding wages and obligations. The legalists, finally, see informal operators as enterprising people who choose to avoid regulation because registration is slow and costly. Each school captures something real, and the most careful empirical work suggests that all three kinds of activity coexist, sometimes within a single street. A woman who sews garments at home for a factory contractor, a boy who repairs bicycles on the pavement and a trader who imports goods and evades customs duties all count as informal, yet their circumstances, their incomes and their prospects could hardly be more different, which is one reason why generalisations about the sector so often mislead.

C. One of the most detailed pictures comes from a six-year study of some four hundred street vendors in the port city of Port Alderon, led by the sociologist Dr Tamsin Okoro-Reyes. Her team found that in good months many vendors earned as much as low-paid formal workers, but that their incomes fluctuated so sharply that few could plan more than a fortnight ahead. More striking was the discovery that apparent disorder concealed elaborate rules. Vendors' associations allocated pitches, settled disputes, and ran rotating savings schemes that functioned as a form of credit. Pitch rights could be inherited, rented or sold, and were respected by people who had never signed a contract. The researchers also noticed that newcomers were rarely excluded outright; instead, they were admitted gradually, first as helpers and then as holders of a small pitch, so that trust was built up over months. Okoro-Reyes concluded that the informal economy is not an absence of institutions but a different set of them, enforced by reputation rather than by courts.

D. The relationship between informal workers and the state is correspondingly ambiguous. Authorities frequently harass vendors through periodic clearances justified by traffic or appearance, yet the same authorities depend on them: civil servants buy lunch from the stalls, and the stalls supply food at prices that keep formal wages affordable. Attempts at formalisation have often failed. In most cities that introduced compulsory registration, take-up was low, since registering brought fees and tax obligations while offering nothing in return. Vendors reasoned that a certificate would not stop their goods being confiscated. The city of Velmora took a different course. It issued a modest licence that attached the holder to a specific pitch and guaranteed a hearing before any removal. Registration there rose sharply within two years, not because the fee was lower, but because the licence finally purchased something worth having: security.

E. Digital platforms have complicated the picture further. Delivery riders and ride-hailing drivers are registered, tracked and rated by companies, yet they usually lack the sick pay, contracts and bargaining rights of employees. Some economists describe this as "formalisation without protection", a reversal of the old expectation in which the paperwork arrives but the benefits do not. At the same time, mobile payment systems have allowed small traders to build records of transactions, which lenders can use to assess creditworthiness, and so give some of them access to loans that were previously unavailable.

F. Policy thinking has consequently moved away from eradication towards integration. Rather than treating informal work as a problem to be removed, many researchers now advocate improving the infrastructure on which it depends: water, storage, lighting and legal recognition of pitches. They also stress the need for distinctions. A widow selling vegetables to feed her children and a workshop owner employing a dozen apprentices have little in common, and a single policy cannot serve both. Nor should the informal economy be romanticised. It also contains hazardous conditions, child labour and exploitation by intermediaries, and the very flexibility that makes it resilient can mean that workers carry risks that no one else will share.

items.text:
A. At first sight, a glacier is the very image of immobility, a frozen landscape that seems to belong to geology rather than to motion. Yet ice is a material that flows. Under sustained stress, the crystals of which it is composed deform and slide past one another, so that a glacier is best imagined as a river whose current is measured in metres per year. The physics of that river has been studied for more than a century, but the questions that matter most today, how fast ice will reach the sea and how much will be lost, depend on details that remain stubbornly hard to observe.

B. The central insight is that the rate at which ice deforms rises steeply with the stress applied to it. Doubling the stress increases the rate of deformation roughly eightfold, a relationship known as a power law with an exponent of about three. Because the stress at the base of a glacier depends on both the thickness of the ice and the slope of its surface, thickness has an outsized effect: for the same slope, ice twice as thick moves about sixteen times faster through internal deformation alone. Most of this deformation is concentrated in the lower layers, where stress is highest, so the upper ice is largely carried along like cargo. A glacier in this idealised state would move fastest at its surface and slowest at its bed, and would respond smoothly to changes in thickness.

C. Real glaciers rarely behave so simply, because the bed matters as much as the ice. The crucial distinction is thermal. In a cold-based glacier, the ice at the bed is below the temperature at which it would melt under pressure, and it is frozen to the rock. Such glaciers move almost entirely by internal deformation, and they are often remarkably effective at preserving the landscape beneath them. In a temperate glacier, by contrast, the base is at the melting point and a thin film of water separates ice from rock. Sliding then becomes possible, and in some temperate glaciers it accounts for most of the observed motion. A single glacier can include both kinds of base, which makes its overall behaviour difficult to predict from surface measurements.

D. The water that lubricates the bed is not a passive ingredient. In summer, meltwater from the surface drains through crevasses and vertical shafts to the base of the glacier. Early in the season the drainage network is inefficient, consisting of narrow, connected cavities. The incoming water raises the pressure at the bed, which partly lifts the ice off its support, and the glacier accelerates. As the season progresses, the flowing water melts larger channels, which carry it away more efficiently and lower the pressure. The paradoxical result is that a glacier may slow down in late summer, when meltwater supply is at its greatest, because the system has become efficient enough to drain it. A few glaciers, known as surge-type glaciers, switch irregularly between decades of slow movement and brief episodes of rapid flow, during which they may advance by many kilometres. The cause of the switch is still debated.

E. Glaciers also have a budget. Snow that accumulates in the upper zone is gradually compressed into firn and then into ice, a process that takes anything from a few years in warm, wet conditions to several centuries in cold, dry ones. Ice that flows to lower elevations is lost by melting, and the line where gains equal losses is known as the equilibrium line. If the climate warms, this line moves uphill and the glacier eventually adjusts by retreating. The adjustment is slow, however. Because ice takes decades to travel the length of a glacier, the terminus responds to climate with a long delay, and a glacier may continue to shrink for many years after temperatures have stopped rising. Its present size therefore reflects an integrated record of past conditions rather than the current climate, which is why a glacier is both a sensitive indicator and a misleading one.

F. Glaciers that end in the sea add a further complication. At such a margin, the ice loses mass by calving, the breaking off of icebergs, and the rate depends on how much resistance the ice meets at its front. If the terminus retreats into deeper water, the cliffs may become so tall that they collapse under their own weight, a hypothesis known as marine ice cliff instability. It has not been conclusively demonstrated, in part because nobody has observed it on the scale required. Satellites can now track the velocity of almost every glacier on Earth, and radar can map the thickness of the ice with some precision. What cannot be seen from above is the condition of the bed, and uncertainty about friction there remains the greatest single obstacle to projecting how much ice will be lost over the coming century.

items.text:
The table shows how much water was used per person each year, in cubic metres, for three purposes in four countries in 2000 and 2020.

Norland: farming 410 (2000), 350 (2020); industry 120 (2000), 95 (2020); households 75 (2000), 88 (2020)
Estavia: farming 160 (2000), 190 (2020); industry 210 (2000), 180 (2020); households 120 (2000), 115 (2020)
Solmar: farming 780 (2000), 810 (2020); industry 40 (2000), 65 (2020); households 35 (2000), 52 (2020)
Tarquin: farming 90 (2000), 70 (2020); industry 150 (2000), 130 (2020); households 140 (2000), 125 (2020)
items.q: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
items.sample:
The table compares annual water use per person for farming, industry and households in four countries in 2000 and 2020. Overall, farming was the largest user in three of the four countries, whereas Tarquin relied more on industry and households, and the most noticeable change was the rise in household use in the two countries with the lowest figures.

Solmar had by far the highest consumption for farming, at 780 cubic metres in 2000 and 810 in 2020, more than double the figure for any other country. Its industrial and household use was tiny by comparison, yet both increased, from 40 to 65 and from 35 to 52 cubic metres respectively. Norland also used most of its water for farming, but the amount fell from 410 to 350, and industrial use dropped from 120 to 95. In contrast, household use there rose from 75 to 88.

Estavia showed a different pattern. Industry was its main user in 2000, at 210 cubic metres, but farming overtook it by 2020, rising to 190 while industry fell to 180. Tarquin recorded the lowest farming figures, 90 falling to 70, and its industrial and household totals declined slightly, from 150 to 130 and from 140 to 125.

items.q: Some people believe that advances in automation will make long working hours unnecessary, so that the working week could be much shorter. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of a shorter working week, and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
items.sample:
It is often claimed that automation will eventually allow people to work far fewer hours without any loss of prosperity. While a shorter working week would bring clear benefits, it also raises difficulties that should not be underestimated, and on balance I believe that a gradual reduction is desirable provided it is carefully managed.

The main advantage is the improvement in wellbeing. Employees who work fewer hours generally report lower stress and better health, and they have more time for family, study and community activities. There is also evidence from several trials that productivity per hour can rise when staff are less tired, so firms do not necessarily lose output. A further benefit is that work could be shared more widely. If machines take over routine tasks, a shorter week would spread the remaining jobs among more people instead of leaving some unemployed while others work excessive hours.

However, the disadvantages are real. In many sectors, such as healthcare, teaching and emergency services, human attention cannot easily be replaced by machines, so shorter hours would mean either more staff or reduced services, both of which are costly. Moreover, the gains from automation are not shared equally. If employers capture most of the savings, workers may see their pay fall along with their hours, and those on low wages would be unable to afford the leisure that the reform is supposed to provide. There is also the risk that people who are accustomed to long hours would simply take a second job.

In my view, the best approach is to reduce hours step by step, starting in industries where automation has already raised productivity, and to protect wages by law. Governments could encourage this through tax incentives and by measuring the results carefully before extending the policy. In this way, society could enjoy the benefits of technological progress without exposing workers to unnecessary risk. In conclusion, a shorter working week is a worthwhile goal, but it should be introduced gradually and fairly.

items.q: Describe a piece of technology that you rely on. You should say: what it is, how long you have used it, what you use it for, and explain why you rely on it so much.
items.sample:
I would like to talk about my smartphone, which is the piece of technology I rely on most. I have used it for about four years, since my parents gave it to me for my fifteenth birthday, and I cannot imagine my daily life without it.

I use it for many different things. In the morning it works as my alarm clock, and on the bus I check the weather and read the news. At school I use it to look up words, record my teacher's explanations and keep my timetable. In the evening I stay in touch with my friends and family, and sometimes I use it to learn English with an app. I also take photos with it, so it is almost like a small camera, a notebook and a library in my pocket.

There are several reasons why I rely on it so much. Firstly, it saves me a lot of time, because I can find information or pay for things within seconds. Secondly, it keeps me connected with relatives who live far away. Finally, it makes me more organised, since it reminds me about homework and appointments. Admittedly, I sometimes spend too much time on it, so I am trying to switch it off an hour before bed. Even so, I would find it very hard to live without it.

items.q: Do you think people depend too much on technology nowadays?
items.sample: I think many people do depend on technology too much. For example, lots of people cannot find their way without a map app, and they forget phone numbers because their phones remember them. However, technology also makes life easier and saves time. In my opinion, the problem is not technology itself, but the fact that we sometimes stop using our own memory and skills.
items.vi: Đánh giá mức độ phụ thuộc vào công nghệ, có ví dụ và đối lập (however).

items.q: How has technology changed the way young people communicate?
items.sample: Technology has changed communication enormously. Young people now communicate by sending messages and photos instead of calling, and they can chat with friends in other countries for free. However, I think that face-to-face conversation has become less common, and some teenagers find it difficult to talk in person. On the other hand, online communication helps shy people make friends more easily.
items.vi: Nêu thay đổi cách giao tiếp của giới trẻ, có mặt tích cực và tiêu cực.

items.q: What problems might be caused by new technologies in the future?
items.sample: In the future, I expect that new technologies will cause several problems. Firstly, machines and artificial intelligence may replace people in many jobs, so workers will need to learn new skills. Secondly, there are privacy risks, because companies collect large amounts of personal data. Finally, people may spend even less time outdoors. Governments and schools should prepare for these changes carefully.

audio.t: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming to the opening of the Westbrook Tool Library. Let me begin with a little history. The idea first came up three years ago, when a group of neighbors realized that most households own a drill that is used for perhaps ten minutes a year. We hoped to base the scheme in the public library, but the council felt that the insurance costs would be too high, so we looked elsewhere. In the end we found this building, the old post office, which had stood empty for years.

Money was the next hurdle. We applied to the council for a grant and were refused, but a local housing charity, the Fenwick Trust, then agreed to cover our first two years of rent and equipment, and that is what made everything possible.

Now, how does it work? Membership costs twenty-five dollars a year, or twelve if you hold a concession card. Members may borrow up to four items at a time for a week, although no more than two of them can be power tools. Before you take away a power tool for the first time, you will need to complete a short safety session. It takes about twenty minutes and is run by our volunteers on the premises, so there is no written test and no deposit.

We have been surprised by what people want. We expected the drills and the ladders to be the favorites, but during our trial period the most requested item was the carpet cleaner, which was out almost every weekend.

For now we are open on Tuesday evenings and Saturday mornings. We would like to add Thursdays, but that depends on having more helpers. Plenty of people have offered to staff the front desk. What we need most at the moment are volunteers who can repair broken tools, because otherwise the equipment will not last.

Looking ahead, from spring we hope to add a garden section, with lawnmowers and hedge trimmers. Lending kitchen equipment is another idea, but that is for the following year at the earliest. Now, please do look around, and I will be happy to answer any questions.

audio.t: Come in, both of you. Let's talk about your project on noise and concentration in open-plan offices. Where have you got to?
We have decided to run an experiment rather than use a questionnaire, because people's reports of how distracted they feel are not very reliable.
I originally wanted a survey of local office workers, since it would give us a much larger sample, but I can see her point.
Both have merit, but an experiment lets you control the variables. How many participants are you planning?
Sixty, in groups of six.

That is more than you need. With two conditions, forty would give you adequate power, and it will save you scheduling headaches. I would recruit first-year psychology students, which is common, but remember to discuss the limitation that students are not office workers, so your results may not apply to them.
We would play a recording of conversation in one condition and have silence in the other, while they do a proofreading task.

Proofreading is sensible, because it is sensitive to distraction. But you must vary the order. If everyone does the quiet condition first, practice may improve their scores in the second, and you would not know whether the noise or the practice caused the difference.
So half of them would hear the noise first.
Exactly.
We also wondered about adding music as a third condition.
I would leave it out. You only have one semester, and it adds complexity. You could suggest it as a direction for further research in your conclusion.
We tried a pilot with five friends. We expected the recording to be a mild distraction, but it was far too loud at sixty-five decibels and people complained, so we lowered it.

Good. Report the pilot in your method section, because it explains why you chose your final volume. Now, you will need approval from the departmental ethics committee. It takes about two weeks, so submit the application by this Friday, with a debriefing sheet.
We had planned to use a spreadsheet for the analysis.
A statistics package is more reliable for comparing the same people across two conditions, and the university runs a workshop on it next Wednesday. I suggest you both go.
And the presentation?
Fifteen minutes. Do not spend long on the background reading, because your audience will know it. Concentrate on why you designed the study the way you did.
Thank you, that is very helpful.
Bring a draft of the method section when we meet in two weeks.

audio.t: Today I want to talk about the history of glassmaking, one of the oldest human technologies. Natural glass, such as obsidian formed in volcanic eruptions, was used for blades long before people made glass themselves. The earliest man-made glass appeared in Mesopotamia around 3500 BC, mostly as colored beads.

The basic ingredient is sand, which is mainly silica, but silica melts only at extremely high temperatures. Early craftsmen discovered that adding a flux, such as soda from plant ashes, lowered the melting point. A third ingredient, lime, was added to make the glass stable, because without it the glass slowly dissolves in water.

For about two thousand years, glass vessels were made by winding soft threads of glass around a core of clay and dung. Then, in the first century BC, glassmakers in the Roman Empire invented blowing. A blob of molten glass was gathered on the end of a hollow iron pipe and inflated like a bubble, which made production much faster and much cheaper.

After the fall of Rome, the center of fine glassmaking moved. By the thirteenth century Venice dominated the trade. In 1291 the glassmakers were ordered to move to the island of Murano, officially because of the danger of fire, though many historians think the real aim was to protect their trade secrets.

The Venetians were famous for cristallo, a very clear glass, and for mirrors, which were made by coating a sheet of glass with a thin layer of tin and mercury. Later, in 1674, an English maker named George Ravenscroft added lead oxide to the mixture, producing a heavy, brilliant glass that is still used for fine tableware.

items.text:
A
Few proposals in the study of language have proved as seductive, or as persistently misrepresented, as the idea that the language we speak shapes the way we think. In its strongest form, sometimes called linguistic determinism, the claim is that the categories of a language set hard limits on what its speakers can conceive. Almost no serious scholar now defends this view. What survives, under the more modest label of linguistic relativity, is the suggestion that habitual patterns of speech may nudge attention, memory and judgment in particular directions, without ever making other ways of thinking impossible. The history of the field is largely the story of a slow retreat from the first claim to the second, and of the ingenuity required to test the latter.

B
The determinist position owed much of its early appeal to anecdote. Commentators delighted in lists of exotic vocabulary, of which the most famous was the supposed abundance of words for snow among Arctic peoples. Careful examination later showed that the figure had been inflated by repetition, and that the languages concerned built their snow terms from a small number of roots, much as English builds compound nouns. The episode left a lasting lesson: differences in vocabulary are easy to observe but hard to interpret. A language may lack a single word for a concept while still expressing it perfectly well in a phrase, and speakers who possess a rich specialist lexicon, such as skiers or wine merchants, are plainly not thereby locked into a different way of seeing the world.

C
Experimental work over the last three decades has therefore looked for subtler effects. One productive line concerns how languages carve up space. Many languages, including English, describe the location of objects mainly in relation to the speaker's own body: the cup is to the left of the plate. A smaller number rely instead on fixed compass directions, so that a speaker might say the cup is to the north of the plate, or warn a visitor that there is an ant on their south-west leg. Researchers working with an upland community of the second type, which they called the Tarrow Valley people, found that when participants were asked to arrange picture cards to show the passing of time, they set them out from east to west regardless of which way they were facing, whereas English-speaking participants arranged them from left to right. The team concluded that constant use of absolute directions had trained these speakers to maintain a continuous sense of orientation, one that most of us lose within moments of entering a windowless room.

D
Color has offered another testing ground. Languages divide the spectrum differently; some distinguish only two basic color terms, others a dozen. Russian, for instance, obliges its speakers to choose between two terms for what English calls blue, one for lighter and one for darker shades. In a widely discussed set of experiments, speakers of such languages were faster at telling two shades apart when they fell on opposite sides of a lexical boundary than when they fell on the same side. Crucially, the advantage vanished when participants had to repeat a string of digits while performing the task, which suggests that language influenced perception only when the verbal system was free to participate. Critics countered that the effects were small, fragile and not always replicated, and that they might reflect nothing more than participants consciously applying a label. Defenders replied that a modest, automatic bias is precisely what a relativist should expect.

E
A third area concerns grammatical features that force speakers to attend to information that others may omit. Some languages oblige a speaker to mark, on every verb, whether the information was witnessed directly or merely reported, so that a casual remark about yesterday's weather commits the speaker to a stance on evidence. Speakers of languages that assign grammatical gender to inanimate nouns have been reported to describe objects in ways that echo the gender of the word: a bridge, grammatically feminine in one language and masculine in another, is called elegant or slender by the first group and sturdy or towering by the second. Yet such findings are open to the objection that the task may have invited participants to rely on the word itself, so that the result tells us about the experimental situation rather than habitual thought. A study in which participants learned invented gender labels for unfamiliar objects, and then showed similar associations within a single afternoon, is sometimes cited as proof that the effect can be created quickly. That cuts both ways: it shows that language can influence association, but it also suggests that the influence is shallow and easily overwritten.

F
The central methodological difficulty is the problem of causation. Speakers of different languages typically also differ in culture, schooling and environment, so any divergence in behavior might stem from these factors rather than from grammar. Researchers have responded in two ways. One is to study bilinguals, whose performance appears to shift according to the language of testing; the other is to train people in a new linguistic habit, as in the invented-gender study, and observe the consequences. Neither strategy is free of flaws, but together they have made the strongest versions of the sceptical position, that language has no measurable influence at all, harder to sustain.

G
What, then, can be concluded? Most researchers would now accept that language is one influence among many on cognition, operating mostly at the margin and on tasks that involve attention, memory or rapid categorization. This is a more modest result than the early enthusiasts hoped for, but it is not trivial. If the language we speak can alter even slightly how we notice, remember and sort the world, then the diversity of human languages is not merely a curiosity of communication but a reservoir of cognitive variety, and the disappearance of a language may represent the loss of more than a vocabulary.

items.q: Almost all serious scholars today accept that language sets hard limits on thought.

Languages with fewer words restrict thought

The experiments used too few languages

items.text:
A
Economists rarely agree on much, but on one point there is something close to consensus: if the damage done by greenhouse gas emissions is not reflected in the prices people pay, emissions will be higher than is socially optimal. The atmosphere is a classic common resource, free to use and therefore overused. The remedy, in theory, is to attach a price to each tonne emitted, so that the cost of the harm is borne by those who cause it. Governments have two main ways of doing so. A carbon tax fixes the price and lets the quantity of emissions adjust; a trading scheme fixes the quantity and lets the price adjust. The second approach has proved politically more appealing, partly because it avoids the word tax, and it has given rise to a bewildering array of markets whose workings and merits are widely misunderstood.

B
In a compulsory, or compliance, market, a regulator sets a cap on total emissions from a group of covered industries and issues tradable allowances that sum to the cap. A company that emits more than its allowance must buy extra permits; one that cuts emissions cheaply may sell its surplus. In principle, abatement then occurs wherever it is least expensive, and the cap can be lowered over time to tighten the overall constraint. In practice, design flaws can be damaging. The first phase of the Northern Estuary scheme handed out too many allowances on the basis of inflated industry forecasts, and when a recession reduced output, a glut of permits sent prices close to zero for several years. Subsequent reforms, which withdrew surplus allowances into a reserve and steepened the annual decline of the cap, restored the price signal, but the episode showed that a market is only as stringent as the quantity that regulators choose to allow.

C
Alongside compliance schemes has grown a voluntary market, in which companies, institutions and individuals buy carbon credits to compensate for emissions they have not eliminated. Each credit is meant to represent one tonne of carbon dioxide avoided or removed elsewhere, through projects as varied as protecting forest, distributing efficient cooking stoves or capturing methane from landfills. Since no regulator compels the purchase, the market depends heavily on trust, and that trust rests on three tests. A credit must be additional, meaning that the reduction would not have occurred without the revenue from its sale; it must be permanent, meaning that the stored carbon will not soon be released again; and it must not cause leakage, in which the polluting activity merely relocates.

D
Additionality is the hardest of the three to verify, because it requires comparison with a counterfactual that, by definition, cannot be observed. Project developers estimate what would have happened in the absence of their intervention, typically how much forest would have been cut down, and are paid for the difference. The incentive to exaggerate the threat is obvious. An independent audit of thirty forest-protection projects, led by the analyst Marit Solheim, found that the baselines used overstated the risk of clearance so consistently that the number of credits issued was, on average, roughly three times what the evidence could justify. Some developers had drawn their baselines from regions with far higher rates of deforestation than the area they were protecting. The auditors did not allege fraud; they argued instead that the methodologies gave developers wide discretion and no reason to use it conservatively.

E
Permanence and leakage raise further difficulties. Trees store carbon only as long as they stand, and a fire or a drought-induced die-back can return decades of sequestered carbon to the air in a matter of days. Many standards therefore require projects to set aside a share of their credits in a communal buffer pool, which is drawn upon if reversals occur. Yet the buffer is calibrated to historical risk, and climate change is steadily making the past an unreliable guide. Leakage is harder still to track: if loggers are barred from one concession, they may simply move to a neighboring one that is unprotected, so that the net gain is smaller than the credits suggest. Methods to estimate such displacement exist, but they rely on assumptions about where and how far activities move.

F
The response to these weaknesses has been a wave of integrity initiatives. Ratings agencies now grade credits against quality criteria, satellite monitoring has reduced reliance on self-reporting, and some buyers have shifted toward removal credits, which pay for carbon actively taken from the atmosphere rather than for emissions avoided. These are more costly, since direct capture technologies currently charge many times the price of a forest credit, but their accounting is simpler and the carbon is easier to measure. Critics remain unconvinced. They argue that even high-quality offsets create a moral hazard, allowing firms to postpone the harder work of changing their own operations, and that a claim to be net zero through purchased credits conflates two very different things: emissions that are cut and emissions that are merely compensated. Defenders retort that offsets channel finance to regions that would otherwise receive none, and that purists risk making the best the enemy of the good.

G
What can be concluded? Carbon markets are neither the panacea their enthusiasts claim nor the sham their detractors allege. They are instruments, and like any instrument their value depends on how they are built and used. Compliance markets work when the cap is tight, credible and tightened on schedule; voluntary ones work when baselines are conservative, data are open to inspection and credits are treated as a supplement to, rather than a substitute for, reductions at source. Where these conditions are absent, a market can create the appearance of progress while the atmosphere registers none.

parts.instr: Questions 27-40. Read the passage and answer the questions.
parts.instrVi: Câu 27-40. Đọc bài và trả lời câu hỏi.

items.text:
A
When a species is domesticated, the transformation is usually obvious in the bones. Cattle, sheep and goats shrank markedly after humans began to herd them, their horns altered and their skeletons became more slender, and archaeologists can use these changes to date the transition with some confidence. The horse is a frustrating exception. Early domestic horses were not appreciably smaller than their wild relatives, and for much of the twentieth century the date and place of the first domestication were matters of fierce and inconclusive argument. The problem has been, in effect, one of recognizing a revolution that left almost no trace in the skeleton, and its solution has required researchers to combine techniques from archaeology, chemistry and genetics.

B
Archaeological approaches have focused on evidence of how animals were used. One method examines the teeth of ancient horses for wear caused by a bit, the bar that sits between the front and back teeth of a ridden or driven animal. A microscopic study led by the zooarchaeologist Tomas Reyes demonstrated that bit wear produces characteristic bevelling of the lower premolars, though it also showed that organic bits of leather or rope can leave very faint marks, making the evidence hard to interpret. A second method analyzes residues in pottery: the presence of fats from mare's milk, identified through their chemical signatures, would imply that horses were being kept and milked rather than merely hunted. A third looks for physical structures, such as enclosures in which the soil has been enriched by dung.

C
For many years the most celebrated evidence came from a settlement on the Kazakh steppe, occupied about 5,500 years ago by a community of hunters who took horses in extraordinary numbers. Horse bones account for the great majority of animal remains at the site, and pits resembling corrals, together with traces of milk fat in pottery, persuaded many scholars that the inhabitants kept domestic herds. The picture seemed settled until genetic analysis intervened. When researchers sequenced the genomes of horses from the site, they discovered that these animals were not the ancestors of the horses that people ride today. Instead they were the forebears of the Przewalski's horse, long regarded as the last truly wild horse but now revealed to be a feral descendant of animals once managed by people. The Kazakh experiment had been real, but it had been a dead end.

D
The genetic search for the true ancestors of modern horses led westward. A survey of several hundred ancient genomes, assembled by an international team directed by Ilse Varga, indicated that the lineage to which almost all present-day domestic horses belong first appeared in the region north of the Black Sea and the Caspian about 4,200 years ago, and then spread across Eurasia with startling speed. Within a few centuries it had almost entirely replaced the local populations, from Western Europe to Mongolia. Such a rapid sweep is unusual: wild horse populations in different regions had remained distinct for tens of thousands of years, and nothing in the earlier genetic record had hinted that one population would overwhelm the rest.

E
Why should this lineage have been so successful? The Varga team noticed that it carried distinctive variants at several genes, two of which are associated with skeletal development, including the strength of the back, and with behavior. One interpretation is that early breeders deliberately selected animals with sturdy spines that could bear a rider's weight and with calm temperaments that made them manageable. It is an attractive hypothesis, but it must be handled with care, for the same variants might have spread for other reasons, and the function of many of the genes involved is still poorly understood. Husbandry itself offers a further clue. Horses breed slowly and, because stallions are quarrelsome, a population can be expanded rapidly only if a few males sire large numbers of foals. The data suggest that exactly such a bottleneck occurred, with a limited number of stallions contributing disproportionately to subsequent generations.

F
The question of what the horse was first used for remains open. Some scholars argue that riding came first, citing skeletal changes in the hips and vertebrae of herders buried about 5,000 years ago, which they interpret as signs of regular time on horseback; sceptics reply that such changes may result from other activities, such as long-distance wagon travel. Wheeled vehicles drawn by horses, in the form of light, spoke-wheeled chariots, appear in the archaeological record around 4,000 years ago, and the military and prestige value of such machines is likely to have encouraged breeders. Whatever the sequence, the consequences were profound: the horse enlarged the distances over which people could travel, trade and fight, and shifted the balance of power between mobile and settled societies.

G
Yet significant gaps remain. The earliest stages of the domestic lineage, the period during which people first learned to control and breed these animals, have not been located in the archaeological record, and the geographical origin of the lineage is inferred from patterns of descent rather than from a single excavated site. Some researchers suspect that the key transition took place in a small, mobile community that left little durable evidence. If so, the final chapter in the story of the horse may be written not with new excavations but with ever more sophisticated analysis of ancient DNA from specimens already sitting in museum drawers.

parts.instr: Writing Task 1. You should spend about 20 minutes on this task. Write at least 150 words.
parts.instrVi: Bài viết 1. Dành khoảng 20 phút. Viết ít nhất 150 từ.

items.text:
The table shows the average number of minutes per day that adults in four countries spent on three leisure activities in 2000 and in 2020.

Norland: reading 42 (2000) and 25 (2020); watching video 95 and 160; outdoor exercise 18 and 31.
Estavia: reading 30 and 22; watching video 120 and 175; outdoor exercise 12 and 15.
Kordova: reading 55 and 38; watching video 80 and 130; outdoor exercise 25 and 20.
Tamerin: reading 20 and 18; watching video 110 and 140; outdoor exercise 9 and 22.
items.q: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
items.sample:
The table compares how much time adults in four countries devoted to reading, watching video and outdoor exercise in 2000 and 2020. Overall, video viewing rose everywhere, while reading declined in every country.

Video was the most significant change. In Norland, daily viewing climbed from 95 to 160 minutes, and Estavia reached the highest figure of 175 minutes, compared with 120 twenty years earlier. Kordova recorded the lowest totals, but even there viewing increased from 80 to 130 minutes.

Reading moved in the opposite direction. Kordova started with the longest reading time, 55 minutes, but fell to 38, whereas Tamerin began and ended at the lowest level, dropping only slightly from 20 to 18. Norland lost 17 minutes, the second largest decline after Kordova.

Outdoor exercise showed a mixed picture. It more than doubled in Tamerin, from 9 to 22 minutes, and rose substantially in Norland, from 18 to 31. By contrast, Estavia saw only a small increase, and Kordova was the sole country where exercise fell, from 25 to 20 minutes.
items.vi: Bài tả bảng số liệu: nêu xu hướng chung (xem video tăng, đọc sách giảm), so sánh các nước và số liệu nổi bật.

parts.instr: Writing Task 2. You should spend about 40 minutes on this task. Write at least 250 words.

items.q: Some people believe that museums and galleries should be free for everyone, while others think that visitors should pay entrance fees. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
items.sample:
The question of whether public museums and galleries should charge admission divides opinion. Some argue that access to culture is a right, while others see fees as a practical necessity. In my opinion, a balanced approach is best.

Those who favor free entry make a strong case. Museums hold collections that belong to society, and charging for them tends to exclude people on low incomes, who may need cultural institutions most. Free admission can also encourage spontaneous visits, for example from students or families, who might not otherwise commit to a ticket price. Evidence from several cities suggests that when fees are removed, attendance rises sharply, and the new visitors are often younger and more diverse.

On the other hand, supporters of fees point out that museums are expensive to run. Conservation, security and research all require stable funding, and government budgets are often under pressure. Ticket revenue provides an independent income, which can protect collections from sudden cuts. Furthermore, some people argue that a modest price encourages visitors to value what they see and to spend more time over it.

However, I believe that neither extreme is satisfactory. A sensible compromise would be to keep permanent collections free, since these are the heart of a public institution, while charging for special exhibitions that cost more to stage. Residents on low incomes could receive discounts, and international tourists, who contribute little to local taxes, might pay a standard fee. Such a system protects access and still raises money.

In conclusion, although fees can supplement funding, the core of a museum should remain open to everyone, because the benefits of culture are shared by the whole community.

parts.instr: Part 2. Speak for one to two minutes on the topic on the card.

items.q:
Describe a building that you find impressive.
You should say:
- where it is
- what it looks like
- when you first saw it
and explain why you find it impressive.
items.sample:
I would like to talk about the main railway station in my city, which I find truly impressive. It stands in the middle of the old town, just a short walk from the river, so almost everyone passes it at some point.

The building is very large, with a high glass roof supported by thin iron arches. Inside, the hall is bright because the light pours through the roof all day, and there is a huge clock hanging above the platforms. The outside is made of pale stone, and there are carved figures above the entrance that represent travel and trade.

I first saw it when I was about eight years old. My grandfather took me there to watch the trains, and I remember being amazed by how high the ceiling was. I felt very small, but also excited, as if the station were a kind of cathedral for travelers.

I find it impressive for several reasons. First, it combines beauty with practical use, because thousands of people use it every day, yet it still feels elegant. Second, it was built more than a hundred years ago, and the engineers managed to create such a wide space without modern machines. Finally, it holds personal memories for me. Whenever I return after a long trip, the sight of that roof makes me feel that I am home.

items.q: Do you think old buildings should be preserved, or replaced by modern ones?
items.sample: In general I think old buildings should be preserved, because they give a city its character and connect people with the past. However, when a building is unsafe or cannot be adapted for modern use, replacing it may be the more sensible option. The best approach is probably to keep the facade and renovate the inside.
items.vi: Bảo tồn hay thay thế công trình cũ: nêu quan điểm và ngoại lệ.

items.q: How does the design of a city affect the way people live?
items.sample: Design affects people in many ways. If a city has wide pavements, parks and good public transport, people tend to walk more and meet each other, which improves health and community spirit. By contrast, cities built around cars can feel noisy and isolating, so people spend more time indoors and rarely talk to neighbors.
items.vi: Thiết kế đô thị ảnh hưởng đến lối sống.

items.q: Should governments spend public money on famous landmark buildings?
items.sample: It depends on the situation. A landmark can attract tourists and become a symbol of pride, so the money may eventually be recovered. However, governments should not spend huge sums on prestige while schools and hospitals lack funding. In my view, the priority should be useful public services, with landmarks funded partly by private investors.
items.vi: Chi tiền công cho công trình biểu tượng: cân nhắc lợi ích và thứ tự ưu tiên.

audio.t: Fernhill Apiary and Learning Centre, good morning. How can I help?
Good morning. I'm calling about the beginners' beekeeping course I saw advertised. Is there still space?
There is, yes. Could I take your surname first?
It's Wendell. That's W-E-N-D-E-L-L.
Thank you, Mr. Wendell. The course runs over six Saturdays, and the first session is on the ninth of March.
Ah, I thought the course began on the sixteenth.
That was last year's. This year we start on the ninth. Each session begins at ten, and finishes at three in the afternoon, although the first day usually ends a little earlier, at two.
And how much is it?
The fee is 185 pounds. It was 150 until last year, but we now include a protective suit, a veil and a hive tool.
Do I need to bring anything?
Boots, please. Rubber ones, because the grass is often wet. Many people bring gloves too, but we would rather you didn't, because they make it hard to handle the frames gently.
Where do the practical sessions take place?
At the hives in the old orchard behind the main building. The classroom is used only when it rains.
Right. Could you send me some details?
Certainly. What's your address?
It's 17 Quarry Road, in Haverstone.
Is that Q-U-A-R-R-Y?
Yes, that's right.
And may I ask how you heard about the course?
I read about it in the local newspaper, although my neighbor mentioned it as well.
Lovely. To confirm your place we need payment within a week. You can pay by card online, but most people send a cheque.
A cheque is fine. Thank you very much.

parts.instr: Questions 11-20. Listen to a talk about a community seed library and choose the correct answer.
parts.instrVi: Câu 11-20. Nghe bài nói về một thư viện hạt giống cộng đồng và chọn đáp án đúng.

audio.t: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to the launch of the Millbrook Seed Library. I'm Priya, and I'd like to explain how it works.

The idea began three years ago among the allotment holders on Cutler Lane. Many of them were growing the same few varieties of bean, bought from the same few suppliers, yet several older members remembered varieties from their childhood that you simply cannot buy any more. They worried that, once those plants disappeared from their plots, the varieties would be lost for good. Saving money was never the point, although it is a pleasant side effect.

The library is housed in the old card catalogue cabinet in the public library, which was donated when the catalogue went digital. We had hoped to use the community center, but its hall is booked every evening. Each drawer holds envelopes of seeds sorted by type, and each envelope carries a label with the name of the grower and the year of harvest.

Membership is free, but there is one rule. You may borrow up to five packets each season, and in autumn you are asked to bring back seed from the plants you have grown. You don't have to return the same quantity as you borrowed, and nobody will check; even a small handful keeps the system alive.

Of course, some crops are far easier to save seed from than others. Beans, peas and lettuce are the simplest, because they pollinate themselves and so stay true to type. Tomatoes are almost as easy, though they need to be fermented to remove the jelly around the seed. Squashes are the opposite. Insects carry pollen from one variety to another, so seed from a squash grown near a courgette, say, may produce something quite unexpected.

That is why we accept squash seed only if the donor grew a single variety that year, or pollinated the flowers by hand. It is a strict rule, and a few people have been disappointed, but the alternative is a drawer full of mysteries.

We held a trial exchange evening in June, and I'll be honest, we expected around twenty people. In fact more than ninety arrived, and we ran out of tables. We had to move the second half of the evening outside, which was fine until it rained.

Another surprise concerned quality. Every donation is tested in spring, by sowing twenty seeds on damp paper. About one packet in ten germinates poorly, usually because the seed was stored somewhere warm and damp. So we now give every donor a leaflet on storage, and we recommend a cool cupboard, not a kitchen shelf.

Our biggest challenge now is not seed, it is people. Cataloguing takes hours, and at the moment just four volunteers do it all. Funding is secure for two years thanks to a grant from the parish council, and the library building costs us nothing, so what we need is time.

Next month we will start a series of workshops, and the first, on the fourteenth, will be held at Millbrook Primary School, where the children have their own bean patch. If it goes well, we would like to hold others at the care home on Lister Street.

Finally, a request. At the back of the room there are two tables. One has membership forms; the other has blank envelopes and pens. If you have seed at home, please fill an envelope before you leave, even if you aren't sure what the plant was; our members can usually identify them. And do try the tea; it was made by the allotment society.

parts.instr: Questions 21-30. Listen to two students talking to their tutor about a research project and choose the correct answer.
parts.instrVi: Câu 21-30. Nghe hai sinh viên nói chuyện với giảng viên về một dự án nghiên cứu và chọn đáp án đúng.

audio.t: Come in, both of you, and sit down. I've read your project outline on community gardens, so let's go through it.
Thanks, Dr. Hargreaves. We wanted to check that the research question isn't too broad.

It's actually the opposite of a problem. Asking whether gardens make neighbors happier would be far too vague, but your narrower version, whether people who take part in a garden know more of their neighbors by name, is measurable. Keep it.
We picked the Ashgrove district because it has three gardens within a short walk, so we can compare people who live near a garden with others in the same district.
Sensible. But why not compare it with a district that has no garden at all?
We considered it, but the areas differ so much in age and income that any difference might have nothing to do with gardens.
Good reasoning. That is exactly the confounding problem, and it's a point worth making in your methods section.
My worry is the questionnaire. One item says, Don't you agree that gardens bring people together? Callum thinks it's fine.
I only meant it as a warm-up question.
Nadia is right. It's a leading question, and respondents will tend to agree. Rewrite it neutrally, and put it after the factual ones, not at the start.
How many people do you plan to survey?
Around forty.
That's on the low side if you want to compare groups. I'd aim for a hundred, but I realize you only have six weeks.
If we use an online form as well as going door to door, we could reach seventy or eighty.
Fine, provided you are honest about the limitation in your discussion. A small sample is not a failure; hiding its size is.
We also plan to try the questionnaire on ten friends first.
Good. What do you hope to learn from that?
Whether anyone misunderstands a question, and how long it takes.
Exactly. Timing matters. Anything over fifteen minutes and people stop answering carefully.
I'm a bit nervous about knocking on doors. People may be suspicious.
Go in pairs, and carry a letter from the department explaining the project. And avoid the evenings once it gets dark.
Do we need written consent from everyone?
Not for the questionnaire. A short statement at the top is enough, and answering counts as agreement. But if you record any interviews, you will need signed consent forms.
What if hardly anyone replies to the online form?
Low response is common. Whatever you do, don't make up for it by choosing only the people who seem friendly. That would bias your results far more than a small sample.
For the open comments, we thought of counting how often words like friendly or welcoming appear.
I'd advise against that. Word counts lose the context. Group the comments into themes, and quote a few of them to illustrate each one.
So what should we do before our next meeting?
Send me the revised questionnaire by Friday, and I'll look at it over the weekend. Then you can start the pilot.

It is too vague to be measured
It is too similar to previous projects

items.text: The angle at which the field lines tilt towards the ground depends on ＿
items.vi: Góc nghiêng của các đường sức từ so với mặt đất phụ thuộc vào vĩ độ (latitude).

audio.t: Good afternoon. Today's lecture is about magnetoreception, the ability of animals to sense the Earth's magnetic field. The planet behaves like an enormous bar magnet, and its field lines tilt towards the ground at an angle that depends on latitude, which in principle gives an animal both a compass and a map.

For decades the idea was dismissed as fantasy. Then researchers kept migrating robins in a closed room with no view of the sky. In autumn the birds still hopped restlessly towards the south-west, the direction of their journey. When the experimenters rotated the magnetic field using large coils, the birds changed direction too.

Sea turtles provide an even more striking example. Hatchlings leave the beaches of Florida and swim out into the Atlantic, following a circular route that takes them around the ocean for several years. They learn the magnetic signature of particular places and steer back when they drift off course.

Salmon do something similar. Born in a small stream, they travel to the open ocean, and after about three years they return to breed in the very same river. They appear to use the magnetic field to reach the right stretch of coast, and then rely on smell to identify their home stream.

So how do animals detect the field? One theory involves a protein called cryptochrome, found in the eye. When light strikes it, a chemical reaction takes place which is influenced by magnetism, so a bird may literally see the field as a pattern laid over its normal vision.

Supporting evidence comes from experiments with colored light. Robins kept under red light became completely disoriented, whereas those under blue or green light navigated normally. That suggests that the mechanism needs light of particular wavelengths in order to work.

A second mechanism involves magnetite, a mineral containing iron. Tiny crystals of it have been found in the beaks of pigeons and in the noses of trout, and they may behave like miniature compass needles, turning as the field changes.

Sometimes the evidence is surprising. Satellite images of thousands of grazing cattle and deer show that the animals tend to line up along a north-south axis. Most researchers were skeptical at first, but the pattern is consistent across six continents.

Interestingly, the alignment disappears when the animals graze close to power lines, which generate their own magnetic fields and confuse the local signal. That is a useful reminder that human activity can interfere with a sense we barely understand.

Finally, a word of caution. We still cannot say precisely where the receptors are, or how the brain processes the signal. What we do know is that this sense has evolved in many groups, from insects to mammals, which suggests that it is far more widespread than anyone imagined.

parts.instr: Reading Passage: The reproducibility reckoning. Answer questions 1-13.
parts.instrVi: Bài đọc: The reproducibility reckoning. Trả lời câu 1-13.

items.text:
A
In 2011, a respected social psychologist published in a leading journal a series of experiments claiming evidence for precognition, the ability of participants to anticipate random events. The methods were conventional and the statistics orthodox, and that was precisely the problem. If standard practice could produce evidence for a phenomenon that almost no scientist believed in, then something in standard practice must be faulty. The episode, combined with several cases of outright fabrication uncovered in the same period, prompted a collective self-examination that has come to be known as the replication crisis. Its central question was uncomfortable: how many of the findings that fill textbooks would survive if the experiments were run again?

B
An answer of sorts arrived in 2015, when a consortium of more than two hundred researchers attempted to repeat one hundred studies published in three prominent journals. The project's leaders took care to contact the original authors and, wherever possible, to use the original materials. Whereas ninety-seven of the originals had reported statistically significant results, only about a third of the repetitions did, and the average size of the effects was roughly half what had first been claimed. Critics were quick to point out that a failed repetition is not a refutation: differences in sample, setting or procedure might explain the discrepancy, and some original authors argued that the replicators had misunderstood subtle features of their methods. Yet the pattern was too widespread to be dismissed as a series of isolated misunderstandings.

C
Much of the explanation lies in what statisticians call researcher degrees of freedom. A typical experiment involves dozens of small decisions: which participants to exclude, when to stop collecting data, which of several measures to report, how to categorize responses. Each choice is defensible in isolation, but together they allow a determined or merely hopeful analyst to find a significant result in almost any dataset. A celebrated demonstration showed that, by exploiting such flexibility, one could apparently prove that listening to a particular song made students younger. The practice, termed p-hacking, rarely involves deliberate deceit. More often the researcher sincerely believes that the analysis chosen was the sensible one, having arrived at it only after seeing which one worked.

D
Compounding the problem was publication bias. Journals favored novel, positive findings, and scientists, whose careers depend on publication, learned to produce them. Experiments that yielded nothing were quietly shelved, a phenomenon known as the file-drawer problem, so that the published literature came to resemble a highlights reel rather than a fair record. Small samples aggravated matters: a study with few participants is likely to miss real effects, but when it does detect one, that effect is probably exaggerated, because only the largest chance fluctuations cross the threshold of significance. A field built on such studies can accumulate an impressive body of results that is, in aggregate, systematically inflated, and that nobody has any particular reason to doubt until someone tries to build upon it.

E
The reforms that followed have been substantial. Pre-registration requires researchers to specify hypotheses, sample sizes and analysis plans publicly before collecting data, which removes the opportunity to adjust them in light of the results. A format known as the registered report goes further: journals agree to publish a paper on the strength of its question and method, before the outcome is known, thereby neutralizing the incentive to prefer positive results. Open data and shared materials allow others to check calculations, while large collaborations pool laboratories so that a single hypothesis is tested across many sites with samples far bigger than any one team could assemble. Early evidence suggests that registered reports contain null results far more often than conventional articles, which is itself revealing.

F
Not everyone is persuaded that the crisis is as grave, or the cure as straightforward, as its advocates claim. Some scholars argue that psychological phenomena depend on context to a degree that makes exact repetition impossible: a study of attitudes conducted in one decade or country may not transfer to another, and its failure to do so tells us about social change rather than flawed science. Others worry that rigid rules will discourage the exploratory work from which new ideas arise, or that the burden of pre-registration falls hardest on junior researchers with limited resources. There is also the awkward matter of what counts as a successful replication; if the criterion is statistical significance, a replication can fail narrowly while the data remain compatible with the original estimate.

G
What has changed most, perhaps, is the culture. A generation ago, to question a colleague's result was thought discourteous; today, replication attempts are routinely published, and a researcher who shares data is more likely to be admired than suspected. Graduate students are now taught to treat a single striking result with suspicion, and funders increasingly pay for confirmation as well as discovery. Whether this will yield a more trustworthy discipline remains to be seen, since incentives, not intentions, ultimately govern behavior, and the pressure to publish has not vanished. But the episode has at least demonstrated that psychology, in confronting its failings openly, has applied to itself the skepticism it ought to apply to every claim.

parts.instr: Reading Passage: The wood wide web. Answer questions 14-26.
parts.instrVi: Bài đọc: The wood wide web. Trả lời câu 14-26.

items.text:
A
Beneath a forest floor lies a structure that most walkers never imagine: a dense web of fungal threads, or hyphae, running through the soil and wrapping the roots of nearly every tree above. These associations, called mycorrhizas, are among the oldest partnerships on land; fossil evidence suggests that fungi were helping plants colonize dry ground more than four hundred million years ago, before roots as we know them had evolved. Today roughly nine in ten plant species form such partnerships. The fungus extends the reach of the root, mining the soil for phosphorus and nitrogen, and in exchange receives sugars manufactured by the plant through photosynthesis, sometimes as much as a fifth of the carbon the plant fixes.

B
Two main types dominate. Arbuscular mycorrhizas penetrate the cells of the root and are found in grasses, crops and most tropical trees, whereas ectomycorrhizas form a sheath around the outside of root tips and characterize many temperate and boreal species such as pines, oaks and birches. The distinction matters, because the second kind produces the mushrooms and truffles familiar to foragers and is more likely to link the roots of different individuals into a shared network. A single fungal individual may colonize the roots of many trees at once, and a single tree may host dozens of fungal species, so that the underground map resembles less a series of private pipelines than a tangled and overlapping lattice, with no obvious beginning or end.

C
The idea that this lattice does more than feed individual trees entered public consciousness in 1997, when a team in British Columbia reported that carbon labelled with a radioactive isotope had moved between seedlings of two species growing in the same plot. Shaded seedlings, it appeared, received more carbon from their taller neighbors. The finding was dramatized in popular books and documentaries, which spoke of a wood wide web through which mother trees nurtured their offspring and warned neighbors of attack by insects. The imagery was irresistible, and it captured the imagination of foresters, conservationists and, eventually, film-makers, who found in it a ready-made moral about cooperation in nature.

D
Scientists who have since scrutinized the evidence are more cautious. Transfer of carbon through fungal links has been demonstrated, but in many experiments the quantities were small and the route uncertain, because carbon can also travel through the soil as dissolved compounds, or be released by decaying roots and absorbed directly. Establishing that a fungal bridge was responsible requires separating it from these alternatives, typically by inserting mesh barriers of different pore sizes, and such controls are demanding. A 2023 review of the literature found that many of the most striking claims about the benefits of networks rested on a handful of studies, and that some widely quoted statements, such as that most forest carbon flows through the network, had no direct support at all.

E
Even where transfer occurs, its significance is debated. Network members are not necessarily beneficiaries; the fungus itself is an economic agent, apparently capable of allocating resources according to the rate of return. Experiments in which the same fungus was connected to plants with differing sugar supplies suggest that it rewards the more generous partners with extra phosphorus, and may charge higher prices when nutrients are scarce. If so, what looks like altruism between trees may in reality be trade, with the fungus as broker. Evolutionary biologists add that it is difficult to see how natural selection would favor a tree that donates its hard-won sugars to a competitor's seedlings, unless the benefits to its own genes were demonstrable.

F
Whatever the truth about sharing, the networks clearly influence how forests develop. Seedlings that germinate within reach of an established network of the appropriate fungus establish more quickly than those that must wait to acquire their own partners, which may explain why some tree species come to dominate large areas. Disturbance matters as well: clear-felling and intensive tillage destroy hyphal networks, and plantings on such ground often need inoculation with the right fungal partner before they thrive. Conversely, networks may help to transmit harm. Some pathogens, and chemicals produced by invasive plants, appear to spread along the same fungal pathways, so that a connection is a liability as well as an asset.

G
Researchers now generally favor modest claims. Few doubt that mycorrhizal fungi are essential to the nutrition of most plants, nor that they shape the composition of plant communities. What remains unproven is the stronger proposition, that forests behave as cooperative superorganisms in which resources are redistributed for the common good. The conservation argument does not depend on that proposition. Protecting old soils and the fungal communities within them is justified by what is already known, and to insist on a more dramatic story risks discrediting a sound case should the dramatic story fail. The task for the next decade is less to find a hidden brain in the forest than to measure, patiently, what actually passes through the threads.
