parts.instr: Reading Passage: Forty days apart. Answer questions 27-40.
parts.instrVi: Bài đọc: Forty days apart. Trả lời câu 27-40.

items.text:
A
The word quarantine comes from the Venetian quaranta giorni, forty days, and it records an experiment in public health rather than a scientific theory. In 1377 the maritime republic of Ragusa, on the Adriatic coast, ordered that arrivals from plague-stricken regions wait on an islet for thirty days before entering the city; later the period was extended to forty, possibly because of the number's resonance in Christian scripture, possibly because it had been associated with the course of acute disease in ancient medicine. Nobody at the time understood that plague was transmitted by fleas carried by rats; the prevailing view held that it spread through corrupted air, or miasma. Yet isolation worked, to a degree, regardless of the reasoning that was used to justify it.

B
Italian cities refined the practice. Venice established an island facility for the sick and a separate one for the merely suspect; Milan sealed infected houses with their occupants inside; and permanent health boards, staffed by physicians and magistrates, gathered information on outbreaks, issued certificates of health to ships and inspected cargo. These boards were remarkable for their authority. They could burn goods, detain travelers and impose fines, and by the sixteenth century they had become some of the most powerful instruments of the state. The apparatus was costly, and merchants resented every day a vessel spent at anchor, so that enforcement depended on a delicate bargain between commerce and caution.

C
The tension between trade and protection was never resolved, only managed. Ports that imposed strict quarantine risked losing traffic to rivals with laxer rules, and officials were frequently bribed or pressured to shorten detention. Authorities also found that ships' captains had every incentive to conceal sickness on board. Some governments responded by punishing concealment severely, while others tried to reward honesty by shortening the period for ships with clean certificates. The system thus rested as much on trust in documents as on any medical observation, and forged certificates were a recurrent problem, rather as counterfeit banknotes are in any monetary system.

D
The nineteenth century brought both a challenge and a reform. Cholera, which spread from the Ganges delta across the world in successive pandemics, did not respond well to the old methods: it moved too quickly, and its victims sickened too soon after infection for a fixed period of detention to serve any purpose. Critics, notably liberal merchants and some physicians who believed that disease arose from local filth rather than contagion, argued that quarantine was a pretext for protectionism and an affront to liberty. In 1851 the first International Sanitary Conference met in Paris to harmonize regulations, though the delegates disagreed so profoundly about the causes of cholera that the resulting convention was never widely ratified.

E
Bacteriology transformed the argument. When Robert Koch identified the cholera bacillus in 1883, and later researchers traced plague to a bacterium carried by fleas, quarantine acquired a rational basis, and with it, greater precision. Periods could be tailored to the incubation time of each disease; rather than detaining healthy and sick together, inspectors could separate those with symptoms, isolate those who had been exposed, and monitor the rest. The distinction in medical vocabulary between isolation of the sick and quarantine of the exposed dates from this period. Yet the new knowledge did not eliminate injustice: in several ports, quarantine regulations fell disproportionately on immigrants and the poor, who were detained in conditions of squalor while first-class passengers were inspected in their cabins.

F
The twentieth century's most devastating pandemic, influenza in 1918, showed both the potential and the limits of such measures. Some communities that acted decisively, closing schools and banning gatherings before the disease arrived, suffered markedly lower mortality than those that delayed. Historians have drawn attention to a small number of isolated places, notably certain Pacific islands, that escaped almost entirely by enforcing a strict maritime blockade. But the virus was so contagious, and so many carriers were without symptoms, that borders alone proved porous in any location with substantial traffic. Later, smallpox eradication relied less on quarantine than on a strategy of surveillance and containment, in which cases were found, isolated and their contacts vaccinated.

G
Contemporary debate echoes the old ones. Modern public health ethics demands that restrictions on liberty be proportionate, based on evidence, limited in duration and accompanied by support for those affected, principles that sixteenth-century magistrates would have found curiously cautious but which are the fruit of centuries of abuse. Questions that vexed the health boards of Venice, how to secure compliance, how to compensate the detained, how to weigh economic cost against risk, remain unsettled. History suggests that quarantine succeeds not through force but when people believe that its burdens are fairly shared, and that the measures most likely to endure are those whose costs have been openly weighed.

items.text:
The table shows the number of visits (in thousands) to four types of leisure facility in the town of Redfield in 2005 and 2023, together with the average ticket price in each year.

Cinema: 420 visits (2005), 310 visits (2023); average ticket $6 (2005), $9 (2023)
Public pool: 280 visits, 350 visits; average ticket $3, $4
Museum: 90 visits, 160 visits; average ticket $4, $4
Gym: 150 visits, 410 visits; average ticket $8, $11
items.q: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
items.sample:
The table compares attendance at four leisure facilities in Redfield in 2005 and 2023, and the average price of a ticket at each. Overall, the gym and the museum grew sharply in popularity, whereas the cinema was the only facility to lose visitors.

In 2005 the cinema was the busiest venue, attracting 420 thousand visits, followed by the public pool with 280 thousand. The gym and the museum were much less popular, at 150 thousand and 90 thousand visits respectively. Ticket prices ranged from $3 at the pool to $8 at the gym.

By 2023 the picture had changed considerably. Gym attendance almost tripled to 410 thousand, making it the most visited facility, even though its ticket price rose by $3 to $11. Museum visits increased by nearly 80 percent to 160 thousand, and this occurred while the price stayed at $4. The pool also gained visitors, rising to 350 thousand, with only a $1 increase in price. In contrast, cinema attendance fell by a quarter to 310 thousand, while its ticket became 50 percent more expensive.

In summary, higher prices appear to have deterred cinema-goers but not gym members, and the cheaper facilities generally attracted more visitors.

items.q: In many countries, an increasing number of people are choosing to live alone. Is this a positive or a negative development? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
items.sample:
In many countries the number of single-person households has risen steadily over the last few decades. Although this trend carries some social risks, I believe that on balance it is a positive development, provided that society adapts to it.

The most obvious benefit is personal freedom. People who live alone can organize their time, their money and their space as they wish, without the compromises that sharing a home demands. For young professionals this independence often encourages self-reliance and maturity, while for older people it allows them to remain in familiar surroundings for as long as they are able. Moreover, living alone is increasingly a choice made from a position of strength. Greater financial security, especially for women, means that nobody needs to share a home simply to survive, or to remain in an unhappy relationship.

Nevertheless, there are genuine drawbacks. Loneliness is the most serious: research consistently links social isolation with poorer mental health and even shorter life expectancy, and people who live alone may have nobody nearby when they are ill. There are also economic and environmental costs. A household of one uses more energy, land and materials per person than a household of four, and a rising number of small homes puts pressure on housing markets, particularly in expensive cities.

However, these problems are not inevitable consequences of living alone, and they can be reduced. Local authorities can design neighborhoods with shared gardens, cafes and community centers that make it easy to meet others. Employers and families can make the effort to stay in contact. A person who lives alone but belongs to a lively network of friends and neighbors is often less isolated than someone in a crowded but unhappy household.

In conclusion, the growth of solo living reflects rising prosperity and personal choice, and it should be welcomed. The responsibility of governments and communities is not to discourage it but to ensure that independence does not turn into isolation.

items.q: Describe a time when you changed your mind about something important. You should say: what you used to believe, what made you change your mind, how you felt about the change, and explain why this experience was significant for you.
items.sample: I would like to talk about the time I changed my mind about studying abroad. Until the age of sixteen I believed that leaving my country would be a mistake. I thought I would be lonely, and I was convinced that a good education was available at home. Then my school organized a two-week exchange program, and my parents encouraged me to apply, although I had my doubts. During those two weeks I lived with a host family, attended lessons in a completely different style and made friends from several countries. At first I felt anxious and homesick, but gradually I realized that I was becoming more independent and more confident. By the end of the trip I had changed my mind completely, and I started to plan to apply for a university overseas. I felt relieved, and a little embarrassed that I had been so certain before. The experience was significant because it taught me not to reject an opportunity simply because it is unfamiliar. It also showed me that changing your mind is not a weakness but a sign that you are learning from experience.
items.vi: Mô tả một lần bạn thay đổi suy nghĩ về điều quan trọng: bạn từng tin gì, điều gì khiến bạn đổi ý, cảm xúc và vì sao trải nghiệm này có ý nghĩa.

parts.instr: Part 3. Discuss the questions with the examiner.
parts.instrVi: Phần 3. Thảo luận các câu hỏi với giám khảo.

items.q: Why do some people find it difficult to change their opinions?
items.sample: I think there are several reasons. Some people feel that admitting a mistake damages their pride, so they defend their opinion even when the evidence is against it. Others simply dislike uncertainty, because holding firm beliefs makes life feel more stable. However, I believe that people who can change their minds are usually more respected in the long run.
items.vi: Giải thích vì sao nhiều người khó thay đổi quan điểm: lòng tự trọng, nỗi sợ bất định.

items.q: Do you think people become more or less willing to change their minds as they get older?
items.sample: It depends on the person, but in general I think people become less flexible with age. Older people have more experience, so they trust their own judgment, and their habits are stronger. On the other hand, experience can also make people wiser and more open to different views. Young people change their minds quickly, but not always for good reasons.
items.vi: Bàn về việc con người dễ hay khó đổi ý hơn khi lớn tuổi, có so sánh hai mặt.

items.q: How can the media or the internet influence what people believe?
items.sample: The media and the internet have a huge influence because most people get their information from them. Social media in particular shows us content that matches our existing opinions, so we rarely hear the other side. This can make beliefs stronger, even when they are wrong. To avoid this, people should check several sources before forming an opinion.
items.vi: Thảo luận ảnh hưởng của truyền thông và internet đến niềm tin của con người.

audio.t: Good morning, Pelham Bay Sailing School. How can I help you?
Hello. I'd like to book a course for my daughter, please.
Certainly. Could I have your surname first?
It's Whitcombe. That's W-H-I-T-C-O-M-B-E.
Thank you, Mr Whitcombe. And how old is your daughter?
She's thirteen.
That's fine. Our minimum age is twelve. Has she sailed before?
She did a beginners' course last summer, Level 1, so I thought she might go straight to Level 3.
I'm afraid students move up one level at a time. Level 3 needs two full seasons of experience, so Level 2 would be the right one.
All right, Level 2 it is.
It runs for five days. We have a course starting on the fourteenth of July, and another on the fourth of August.
July suits us better, because we're away in August.
Then I'll put her down for the fourteenth of July. Sessions begin at nine each morning and finish at four.
Could she start at eight? We have a long drive.
I'm sorry, the boats aren't rigged before nine, so nine it has to be.
No problem. And what's the fee?
It's two hundred and forty-five dollars. It was two hundred and thirty last year, but prices went up in January.
That's fine. Where do we meet on the first day?
At the boathouse, the blue building beside the slipway. Please don't come to the main office.
And what should she bring?
A waterproof jacket is essential. We provide life jackets and boots, but sun cream and a hat are a good idea too.
Is lunch included?
No, I'm afraid she'll need to bring a packed lunch each day, though there is a cafe where she can buy hot drinks.
Right. And is there anywhere to park?
There's free parking in the Marsh Road car park, about two minutes on foot. The one on Quay Street charges, so I'd avoid it.
Wonderful, thank you very much.

audio.t: Welcome, everyone, and thank you for volunteering at Alderbrook Mill. I'm Carol Hendry, the volunteer coordinator, and I'll spend the next few minutes explaining how the museum works.

The mill was built in 1786 to grind grain using the tide, which fills a large pond at high water and drives the wheel as it drains. It stopped working commercially in 1951, and the building then stood empty for decades, until a local campaign saved it in 1998.

Today we receive about thirty thousand visitors a year, most of them between April and September. Many people assume that school groups are our biggest audience, but in fact retired couples are the largest group, followed by families, with schools only in third place.

Volunteers can choose between three roles. Guides lead tours of the wheel house, shop assistants work in the gift shop, and archive assistants help to catalogue photographs and documents upstairs. We have plenty of guides at the moment, and the shop is fully staffed, but we are short of archive assistants.
Everyone completes a half-day training session. We supply a fleece with the museum logo, but the floor of the wheel house is uneven, so please wear sturdy flat shoes of your own.
Shifts last four hours. Most people do one shift a fortnight, although a few come weekly. The only firm rule is that you must give us a week's notice if you cannot come, so that we can arrange cover.
A word about photographs. Visitors may take pictures everywhere except in the archive room, where old documents are sensitive to light.
Now, safety. The most hazardous area is the mill race, the channel beneath the building. A barrier is being installed, but until it is finished you must never take a group beyond the yellow line.
Next month we launch a new exhibition on the lives of the millers' families. We are looking for volunteers to record interviews with local people who remember the mill at work.
Finally, money. The museum receives no government funding. About half of our income comes from admission fees, a third from the shop, and the rest from donations.
If you would like to start straight away, please see Joanne in the office after this talk. This Thursday's training session is full, so the next one will be on Tuesday morning at ten.

audio.t: Come in, both of you. Now, you wanted to talk about your project on urban pollinators.

Yes, Dr Okafor. We want to compare bee activity in rooftop gardens with activity in ground-level parks, but we're stuck on the method. The biggest difficulty is deciding how to measure activity. Identifying the species is a problem too, but we can photograph the bees and ask a specialist later.
We thought about counting every bee we see, but that seems unreliable, and tagging individual bees is out of the question.
Quite. I'd suggest something simpler. Mark out a one-metre square patch of flowers and count how many bees land on it during ten minutes, at the same times each day.
I did wonder about setting up video cameras instead, so that we wouldn't need to be there.
Ben, we'd end up with dozens of hours of footage and no time to analyze it.
True. I'd forgotten that.

Whichever method you use, weather matters. Bees fly less in wind and cold, so note the temperature and wind speed at every session. You don't need to rule out a day entirely, because you can take conditions into account in the analysis.
We had planned four sites: the two rooftops, the botanical garden and the cemetery.
I'd drop the cemetery. Its flowers are mostly wild grasses and clover, quite unlike the rooftop planting, so any difference you found might be due to the plants rather than the location.
That makes sense. And how many sessions should we do at each site?
At least eight, spread across the season. Five would leave you vulnerable to a couple of freak days.
We had planned five, so we'll extend that to eight. Ten would be too many for our timetable.
Have you spoken to the estates office about the rooftops?
We phoned, but they said we need to put the request in writing.
Then do that before anything else. Without written permission you won't be allowed on the roof, and the department won't cover you for insurance.
For the analysis, I was thinking of using the advanced modelling software.
I'd wait. Start by comparing the average counts at each site in a simple chart. If the differences are clear, you may not need anything complicated.
What about background reading? I found a book from 2009 on pollinators in cities.
Use it for the history, but the field has changed fast. I'd rely mainly on the review article published last year, which includes the newer data.
Right. When would you like to see our plan?
Email me a draft by Friday, and we'll meet again next Wednesday.

audio.t: Good morning. Today I want to talk about the engineering of suspension bridges, which are the longest bridges in the world. The basic idea is simple. The road deck hangs from vertical cables, and those cables are attached to two main cables that pass over tall towers and are anchored firmly at each end. Because the deck is carried by cables in tension rather than by solid supports below, a suspension bridge can cross a gap that no other design can span.

Let us start with the main cables, which carry almost the whole load. Each one is made of thousands of thin steel wires, bundled together in a process called spinning. The wires are so strong that a single cable only a little more than one metre wide can support the weight of the deck and many thousands of vehicles. Engineers choose wire rather than solid steel bars because wire is stronger for its weight and, if one strand fails, the others carry on.

The towers have a different job. They do not hold the deck directly; they simply lift the main cables high enough to form a gentle curve. The weight pressing down on the towers is huge, so they are usually built from reinforced concrete or steel. In a long bridge the towers are also slightly further apart at the top than at the base, a difference of a few centimetres, because the Earth is curved.

Next, the anchorages. The main cables pull horizontally on the ends of the bridge with enormous force, so each end is fixed to a massive block of concrete, often set deep into rock. If the anchorage moved even slightly, the whole shape of the bridge would change. For this reason, the anchorages are often the most expensive part of the construction, and the survey of the ground beneath them can take up to two years.

The most serious danger is not weight but wind. In 1940 a famous bridge in North America twisted and collapsed in a wind of only sixty-four kilometres an hour. Its deck was narrow and solid, and the wind made it vibrate until it broke. Since then, designers test every new bridge as a small model in a wind tunnel. Modern decks are shaped like an aircraft wing and often have slots so that air can pass through, which stops the dangerous vibration.

Bridges must also cope with heat. On a hot day the steel expands, and a long deck can grow by more than a metre. To allow for this, engineers fit expansion joints, which are toothed steel plates that slide past one another, so the road stays smooth while the deck moves. Without these joints, the deck would buckle.

Finally, maintenance. Inspectors use robots to check the inside of the main cables, where moisture causes corrosion. Some bridges now blow dry air through the cables to keep the wires protected, and sensors measure the movement of the deck day and night. For next week, please read the case study on the course page and prepare two questions.

parts.instr: Read the passage on dark matter and answer questions 1-13.
parts.instrVi: Đọc bài về vật chất tối và trả lời câu hỏi 1-13.

items.text:
A. For most of the history of astronomy, the mass of a galaxy was something to be counted rather than argued over. Astronomers photographed the stars, estimated how bright each one was, converted that brightness into mass using what was known about stellar physics, and added a modest allowance for gas and dust. The total, it was assumed, would explain how the galaxy moved. The assumption seemed so natural that it was rarely stated, which is perhaps why its failure, when it came, proved so unsettling. In the 1930s, a few astronomers noticed that galaxies in large clusters were moving far too quickly to be held together by the gravity of their visible matter; the clusters ought to have dispersed long before. The anomaly was acknowledged and then largely set aside, since the measurements were uncertain and few researchers saw a reason to abandon a successful theory of gravity on the strength of a handful of unruly clusters.

B. The decisive evidence came from a more intimate scale: the rotation of individual spiral galaxies. In the solar system, most of the mass is concentrated at the centre, and the planets farthest out move the slowest, because the pull they feel is weaker. If a galaxy's mass were concentrated in its bright central bulge, the same pattern should hold: stars at the rim should orbit more slowly than those near the middle. In the 1970s, careful spectroscopic surveys led by the astronomer Ingrid Solberg and her colleagues showed that nothing of the kind happens. Beyond the inner regions, orbital speeds stay stubbornly flat, sometimes even rising, out to the very edge of the visible disc. The rotation curve, as it is called, refuses to fall. The implication was inescapable. Either there is far more mass in the outer parts of a galaxy than the starlight indicates, or the laws that connect mass to motion need revision.

C. The first reading, that of unseen matter, became known as the dark matter hypothesis, and it has the virtue of conservatism: it leaves gravity untouched and adds only a new ingredient. Calculations indicated that each spiral galaxy must be embedded in a roughly spherical halo of invisible material, extending several times further than the stars and contributing perhaps five times as much mass as all the ordinary matter combined. Dark matter, in this picture, does not emit, absorb or reflect light at any wavelength; it reveals itself only through its gravitational pull. Early proposals that it might consist of ordinary but faint objects, such as dim stars, wandering planets or small black holes, were tested by searching for the brief brightening that such objects would cause as they drifted in front of distant stars. The searches found far too few to matter, and attention shifted to a stranger possibility: a population of undiscovered particles that interact with ordinary matter only very weakly.

D. Support accumulated from directions that had nothing to do with rotation. Gravitational lensing, in which the mass of a foreground cluster bends the light of galaxies behind it, allows astronomers to map where mass sits regardless of whether it shines. The maps consistently show far more mass than the visible matter can supply. The most persuasive case came from the so-called Bullet Cluster. In a collision between two galaxy clusters, the hot gas, which holds most of the ordinary matter, was slowed by friction and left near the centre of the wreckage, while the lensing maps indicated that most of the mass had passed straight through and continued outward. Mass and ordinary matter had been separated, something very difficult to explain if the apparent missing mass were merely a flaw in the law of gravity. Meanwhile, the faint pattern of temperature variations in the radiation left over from the early universe could be reproduced by models only if a large share of the matter were non-luminous and unresponsive to light.

E. Yet the alternative has never been entirely abandoned. Modified gravity theories propose that gravity weakens less rapidly than Newton's law predicts when accelerations are very small, as they are at the outskirts of galaxies. The best known of these, Modified Newtonian Dynamics, reproduces the flat rotation curves of many galaxies remarkably well, and with fewer adjustable parameters than the dark matter approach, which must tune a separate halo for each galaxy. Its supporters point to a tight empirical relationship between the visible mass of a galaxy and its rotation speed, which dark matter models must explain as the outcome of complicated formation processes rather than as a direct consequence of the theory. Critics reply that modified gravity struggles with galaxy clusters, with the lensing evidence and with the cosmic background radiation, and that the extensions devised to deal with these have become so elaborate that the original simplicity has been lost.

F. Direct searches continue. Detectors buried deep underground, shielded from cosmic rays, wait for a dark matter particle to collide with an atomic nucleus and release a flash of light or a tiny quantity of heat. Decades of operation have produced no confirmed signal, steadily excluding the simplest candidates and narrowing the range in which a particle might hide. Some researchers consider this silence a warning; others regard it as the normal pace of a hard experiment. What is at stake is more than a missing ingredient. Whichever account prevails, either a theory of gravity that has served physics for three centuries or a catalogue of the universe that omits most of its matter will have to be revised. Until then, the rotation of galaxies remains a reminder that what astronomers can see is only a minority of what is there.

items.q: Before the 1970s, astronomers generally expected the visible components of a galaxy to account for its mass.
items.vi: Đoạn A: người ta mặc định khối lượng thiên hà có thể tính từ sao, khí và bụi nhìn thấy. Đáp án True.

items.q: According to the author, the failure of the old assumption about galaxy mass was unsettling because
options: it contradicted the behavior of the solar system.
it had been proposed only recently.
the assumption had seldom been openly examined.
it had been tested and confirmed many times.
items.vi: Đoạn A: giả định tự nhiên đến mức hiếm khi được nêu ra, nên sự sụp đổ của nó gây xáo trộn.

items.q: What does the author mean by saying that the rotation curve 'refuses to fall'?
options: The central bulge rotates faster than the outer disc.
The measurements could not be repeated by other teams.
Stars at the rim gradually fall toward the center.
Orbital speeds in the outer galaxy do not decline as expected.
items.vi: Đoạn B: tốc độ quay ở vùng ngoài vẫn phẳng thay vì giảm, trái với dự đoán.

items.q: What did the Bullet Cluster observation demonstrate?
options: Hot gas carries more mass than the surrounding stars.
Most of the mass can be located somewhere other than the ordinary matter.
Dark matter loses speed through friction like gas.
Lensing maps are unreliable for colliding clusters.
items.vi: Đoạn D: khí nóng bị chậm lại còn phần lớn khối lượng đi thẳng qua, tức khối lượng và vật chất thường tách rời nhau.

items.q: What is the author's attitude to the silence of underground detectors?
options: Opinion among researchers is divided about its meaning.
It shows that the experiments are poorly designed.
It has convinced most scientists to abandon the search.
It proves that modified gravity is correct.
items.vi: Đoạn F: một số coi là lời cảnh báo, số khác coi là nhịp độ bình thường của thí nghiệm khó, tức ý kiến chia rẽ.

items.q: Which paragraph mentions an experiment designed to detect a particle directly?
items.vi: Đoạn F nói về các máy dò đặt sâu dưới lòng đất chờ hạt vật chất tối va chạm.

items.q: Which paragraph explains why one early candidate for the missing mass was rejected?
items.vi: Đoạn C: các vật thể mờ bình thường bị loại vì các cuộc tìm kiếm thấu kính vi mô thấy quá ít.

items.q: Which paragraph describes a proposal that gravity behaves differently when accelerations are tiny?
items.vi: Đoạn E: các lý thuyết hấp dẫn sửa đổi cho rằng hấp dẫn yếu đi chậm hơn ở gia tốc rất nhỏ.

items.q: Which paragraph outlines a way of mapping mass using the bending of light?
items.vi: Đoạn D: thấu kính hấp dẫn cho phép lập bản đồ khối lượng dù nó có sáng hay không.

parts.instr: Read the passage on the sociology of trust and answer questions 14-26.
parts.instrVi: Đọc bài về xã hội học của lòng tin và trả lời câu hỏi 14-26.

items.text:
A. Trust is one of those concepts that everyone uses and few can define. Sociologists have long regarded it as the quiet infrastructure of social life: we board trains driven by strangers, deposit wages with institutions we will never see, and eat food prepared by people whose names we do not know, all without investigating the risks. Yet precisely because it works so smoothly, trust tends to attract attention only when it is withdrawn. A bank run, a food scandal or the collapse of a neighborhood into mutual suspicion reveals how much was resting on an unexamined expectation that others would behave as they should. The contemporary sociology of trust began as an attempt to explain that expectation, and it has gradually become a study of how societies manage uncertainty.

B. An influential early account, associated with the theorist Leopold Brandt, treated trust as a response to the limits of knowledge. If we knew with certainty what others would do, there would be no need to trust them; if we knew nothing, trust would be mere folly. Trust occupies the territory between, as a willingness to accept vulnerability on the strength of incomplete information. This formulation had two consequences. It distinguished trust from confidence in routine, because the latter does not involve a choice, and it implied that trust could be rational, in that a person might weigh the likely benefits of cooperation against the cost of being betrayed. Critics objected that few people actually make such calculations, and that rational choice accounts cannot explain why trust so often appears to precede evidence rather than follow it.

C. A second tradition shifted the focus from individuals to relationships. In small communities, trust is anchored in personal history: we trust a neighbor because we have observed her conduct over years, and because her reputation among others would suffer if she cheated us. This is sometimes called thick trust. Modern societies, however, depend overwhelmingly on interactions with strangers, where no shared history exists. Here thin trust, or generalized trust, operates: a readiness to assume that unfamiliar others are, in the main, cooperative. Large surveys carried out across dozens of countries have found striking differences in the level of such trust, with some populations reporting that most people can be trusted and others reporting the reverse. Researchers have proposed that these differences reflect economic equality, the quality of public institutions and even the historical experience of a region, though disentangling cause from consequence has proved exceptionally hard.

D. The question of causation lies at the heart of the debate. One group of scholars argues that generalized trust is a cultural inheritance, transmitted through families and schools and remarkably stable across generations. Evidence for this view comes from studies of migrants: the descendants of people who left a low-trust society tend to retain some of its attitudes decades later, even in a high-trust setting. A rival group maintains that trust is better understood as a rational reading of present conditions. If courts enforce contracts and officials are seldom corrupt, then trusting strangers is a sensible policy; if they do not, suspicion is merely realism. On this account, trust follows institutions rather than the other way round. The evidence that institutional reforms sometimes raise trust within a single generation is cited in support, although such cases are rare and frequently disputed.

E. Digital platforms have introduced a new complication. Rating systems and verified reviews allow strangers to transact with a confidence that, thirty years ago, would have been inconceivable: a traveler will sleep in the spare room of someone she has never met because a score of 4.9 stands beside the host's name. Sociologists describe this as trust mediated by a system, not by acquaintance or by an institution in the traditional sense. Its advocates see an efficient substitute for the slow accumulation of reputation. Skeptics note that ratings are vulnerable to inflation, since reviewers hesitate to leave negative remarks about people they have met, and to manipulation by those who buy favorable comments. More fundamentally, they suggest, trusting a score differs from trusting a person: it transfers confidence to an algorithm whose workings are opaque, and when it fails, the injured party has no relationship to which to appeal.

F. Another strand of research examines what happens when trust is betrayed. Experiments show a pronounced asymmetry: trust is built slowly through many small positive experiences, yet destroyed quickly by a single serious violation. Moreover, the damage depends on the nature of the breach. A failure of competence, such as an adviser who gives mistaken but honest advice, is more readily forgiven than a failure of integrity, such as an adviser who knowingly conceals a conflict of interest. Organizations that understand this distinction tend to recover faster from crises, since they respond to integrity failures with transparency and structural change rather than reassurance. Some scholars go further and argue that moderate distrust, in the form of audits, inspections and a free press, does not oppose trust but sustains it by making betrayal costly.

G. It would be a mistake to conclude that more trust is always better. Excessive trust exposes individuals to fraud and institutions to complacency, and a society in which no one ever checks anything is not a society of virtue but of fragility. The sociological challenge is therefore less to maximize trust than to calibrate it: to ensure that it is extended to those who deserve it and withheld from those who do not. That requires, above all, reliable ways of telling the difference, which brings the discussion back to knowledge, institutions and the information available to ordinary people. Trust, in the end, is not the opposite of skepticism. It is what remains when skepticism has done its work and a decision must still be made.

items.q: Trust usually becomes a subject of public attention when it has been lost.
items.vi: Đoạn A: lòng tin chỉ thu hút sự chú ý khi bị rút lại. Đáp án True.

items.q: Brandt's account treated trust and routine confidence as essentially the same thing.
items.vi: Đoạn B: lý thuyết này phân biệt lòng tin với sự tin cậy theo thói quen vì loại sau không có sự lựa chọn. Đáp án False.

items.q: Surveys of generalized trust have covered more countries than any other sociological survey.
items.vi: Bài chỉ nói các khảo sát bao gồm hàng chục quốc gia, không so sánh với khảo sát khác. Đáp án Not Given.

items.q: Studies of migrants show that attitudes to trust change completely within a single generation.
items.vi: Đoạn D: hậu duệ của người di cư vẫn giữ một số thái độ cũ nhiều thập kỷ sau. Đáp án False.

items.q: Online rating systems may overstate how reliable people are because reviewers tend to avoid criticism.
items.vi: Đoạn E: người đánh giá ngại nhận xét tiêu cực nên điểm số bị thổi phồng. Đáp án True.

items.q: What objection did critics raise against the early rational account of trust?
options: It ignored the cost of being betrayed.
It does not explain why trust often comes before evidence.
It claimed that trust was impossible without certainty.
It confused trust with an emotional attachment.
items.vi: Đoạn B: các nhà phê bình cho rằng lý thuyết lựa chọn hợp lý không giải thích được vì sao lòng tin thường có trước bằng chứng.

items.q: According to the rival group of scholars in paragraph D, suspicion in some societies is
options: a feeling that disappears when surveys are conducted.
a cultural habit inherited from earlier generations.
a result of poor education in schools.
a sensible response to the conditions that people face.
items.vi: Đoạn D: nếu tòa án và quan chức không đáng tin thì nghi ngờ chỉ là thực tế, tức phản ứng hợp lý với điều kiện hiện tại.

items.q: Why do some organizations recover faster from crises, according to paragraph F?
options: They answer failures of integrity with openness and structural change.
They replace their senior advisers as quickly as possible.
They concentrate on proving that their advice was honest.
They avoid admitting that any breach has occurred.
items.vi: Đoạn F: tổ chức hiểu sự khác biệt này đáp lại lỗi về liêm chính bằng minh bạch và thay đổi cơ cấu thay vì trấn an.

items.q: What is the main conclusion of the final paragraph?
options: Ordinary people cannot judge who deserves trust.
Skepticism ought to be removed from public life.
Societies should aim to match trust to trustworthiness.
Trust should be maximized wherever it is possible.
items.vi: Đoạn G: thách thức là hiệu chỉnh lòng tin, trao cho người xứng đáng và giữ lại với người không.

items.q: Which paragraph contrasts trust based on personal history with trust in unfamiliar people?
items.vi: Đoạn C phân biệt lòng tin dày (dựa trên lịch sử cá nhân) và lòng tin mỏng (với người lạ).

items.q: Which paragraph suggests that a form of mistrust can strengthen trust?
items.vi: Đoạn F: sự nghi ngờ vừa phải như kiểm toán, thanh tra, báo chí tự do duy trì lòng tin.

items.q: Which paragraph describes trust being placed in a numerical score?
items.vi: Đoạn E: du khách tin điểm 4,9 bên cạnh tên chủ nhà.

items.q: Which paragraph defines trust as accepting vulnerability on the basis of incomplete information?
items.vi: Đoạn B: lòng tin là sự sẵn sàng chấp nhận tổn thương dựa trên thông tin không đầy đủ.

parts.instr: Read the passage on ancient irrigation societies and answer questions 27-40.
parts.instrVi: Đọc bài về các xã hội thủy lợi cổ đại và trả lời câu hỏi 27-40.

items.text:
A. The image of the ancient river valley as the cradle of civilization has been repeated so often that it has acquired the status of common sense: where there was a great river, there was irrigation, and where there was irrigation, there were surplus harvests, cities and states. The sequence has an appealing logic, but archaeologists increasingly doubt that it describes what actually happened. Irrigation is not one technology but a family of practices, ranging from a farmer scooping water onto a plot to a network of canals extending across a hundred kilometers, and the social consequences of each differ enormously. Treating them as interchangeable has obscured one of the most interesting questions in the study of early societies: did large-scale water management create centralized political power, or did existing power make large-scale water management possible?

B. The first position was articulated most forcefully in the middle of the last century. According to this hydraulic hypothesis, rulers of arid lands could command the labor needed to dig, clean and regulate great canals, and in doing so acquired control over food itself. A class of administrators emerged to schedule water, record labor and collect taxes, and the state grew as the necessary organ of a society that could not survive without coordination. The theory was elegant and, for a time, dominant. It also carried a darker implication, that irrigation tied people to despotic government, since a farmer dependent on a canal could scarcely refuse to obey the authority that managed it.

C. Fieldwork has not been kind to the theory. Detailed surveys of early irrigated landscapes, such as those carried out by the archaeologist Tomasz Reuben on the lowland he calls the Halvane plain, reveal canal systems that grew gradually, in small increments, over many centuries. The earliest channels were short, led water from a stream to a handful of fields, and were plainly built and maintained by local groups of households without any central direction. Only much later, and often after cities had already appeared, do the large canals show up in the record. In several regions, in other words, the state came first. Irrigation, far from creating a ruling class, seems to have been absorbed by a ruling class that already existed, and which then took credit for it.

D. If rulers did not build the first irrigation systems, who did? Anthropologists studying communities that still use traditional gravity-fed channels offer some clues. In the highland valleys of several countries, farmers regulate shared water through rotation schedules, agreed penalties and elected or hereditary water officials, with no state involvement at all. Disputes are settled by neighbors, and those who neglect their obligation to clear silt from a shared channel are sanctioned first by public disapproval and then by fines. These arrangements have survived for generations, which suggests that cooperative management of a common resource, long thought to be fragile, can be stable when the group is small, its members are known to one another, and the boundaries around who may use the water are clear. Some archaeologists believe that comparable institutions operated in ancient times, leaving few written traces precisely because they needed none.

E. This does not mean that irrigation had no political consequences. As systems expanded, new tensions appeared. Farmers at the head of a canal had the first claim on its water, while those at the tail depended on their restraint, and the unequal geography of access created an incentive to seek a powerful patron. Excavated settlements show that, as networks lengthened, storehouses and administrative buildings clustered near the main intakes, suggesting that someone, at some point, began to control the distribution of the harvest. The relationship, then, may have been circular: modest local irrigation allowed larger populations, larger populations required bigger systems, and bigger systems offered ambitious individuals a lever with which to concentrate authority.

F. Environmental evidence adds a note of caution about the benefits of these systems. Irrigating dry land in poorly drained soils draws salts upward, and over centuries the fields of some early societies became so saline that yields fell sharply. Analysis of preserved grain from one southern settlement shows a gradual shift from wheat to the more salt-tolerant barley, a change that scholars interpret as an adaptation, though the shift may also have contributed to the economic decline of the region. The lesson, some argue, is that irrigated agriculture generated its own vulnerabilities, and that the political institutions built to manage it were, in part, responses to a continuing crisis rather than the confident products of surplus.

G. No single explanation now commands general assent. Many specialists favor a more modest view: that water management and political organization developed together, each shaping the other, in ways that varied with climate, terrain and the existing social order. This is a less dramatic claim than the old hypothesis, and it offers no neat law linking rivers to rulers. But it has the merit of agreeing with the evidence, which increasingly depicts ancient irrigators not as passive subjects of an engineering state but as active, inventive communities who negotiated, and sometimes resisted, the terms on which they shared water.

items.q: Many archaeologists now doubt the traditional sequence leading from irrigation to cities and states.
items.vi: Đoạn A: các nhà khảo cổ ngày càng nghi ngờ trình tự quen thuộc này. Đáp án True.

items.q: The hydraulic hypothesis suggested that irrigation encouraged democratic forms of government.
items.vi: Đoạn B: giả thuyết này hàm ý thủy lợi trói buộc con người vào chính quyền chuyên chế. Đáp án False.

items.q: Reuben's survey of the Halvane plain covered more canals than any earlier survey.
items.vi: Bài chỉ nêu Reuben khảo sát đồng bằng Halvane, không so sánh quy mô với khảo sát khác. Đáp án Not Given.

items.q: In some regions the earliest canals were maintained without any central direction.
items.vi: Đoạn C: các kênh đầu tiên do các nhóm hộ gia đình địa phương xây dựng và duy trì, không có chỉ đạo tập trung. Đáp án True.

items.q: Salt damage affected only societies that irrigated well-drained soils.
items.vi: Đoạn F: nhiễm mặn xảy ra khi tưới ở đất thoát nước kém. Đáp án False.

items.q: What is the main point the author makes in paragraph A?
options: Rivers were unimportant to the growth of early states.
Archaeologists have proved that cities came before farming.
Large canal networks were invented before small ones.
The term irrigation covers practices of very different scales, which complicates the question of cause.
items.vi: Đoạn A: thủy lợi gồm nhiều hình thức với quy mô khác nhau, nên câu hỏi về quan hệ nhân quả bị che mờ.

items.q: What does paragraph C suggest about large canal systems?
options: They were designed by the first ruling class.
They were built to make cities possible.
They often appeared after cities already existed.
They replaced the local channels within a few years.
items.vi: Đoạn C: các kênh lớn xuất hiện muộn, thường sau khi các thành phố đã hình thành.

items.q: According to paragraph D, cooperative management of shared water can last when
options: the group is small and its members know one another.
the water supply is greater than the demand.
written laws are kept in a temple archive.
a central authority punishes every offense.
items.vi: Đoạn D: sự quản lý hợp tác bền vững khi nhóm nhỏ, các thành viên quen biết nhau và ranh giới sử dụng rõ ràng.

items.q: Why might farmers at the tail of a canal have sought a powerful patron?
options: They relied on the self-restraint of those upstream.
They lived too far from the storehouses.
They wanted to avoid paying fines for cleaning silt.
items.vi: Đoạn E: nông dân ở cuối kênh phụ thuộc vào sự tiết chế của người ở đầu kênh nên có động cơ tìm người bảo trợ.

items.q: How does the author regard the modest view described in paragraph G?
options: It proves that irrigators resisted all rulers.
It has been rejected by most specialists.
It is as elegant as the hydraulic hypothesis.
It is less dramatic than the old theory but fits the evidence better.
items.vi: Đoạn G: quan điểm khiêm tốn kém ấn tượng hơn nhưng phù hợp với bằng chứng.

items.q: Which paragraph mentions a change of crops as a response to environmental damage?
items.vi: Đoạn F: chuyển từ lúa mì sang lúa mạch chịu mặn hơn.

items.q: Which paragraph describes how disputes over shared water are settled without the state?
items.vi: Đoạn D: tranh chấp được hàng xóm giải quyết bằng lịch luân phiên, hình phạt đã thỏa thuận và các quan chức nước.

items.q: Which paragraph challenges the idea that all irrigation had the same social effects?
items.vi: Đoạn A: thủy lợi là một họ các thực hành với hệ quả xã hội rất khác nhau.

items.q: Which paragraph refers to physical evidence that someone controlled the storage of the harvest?
items.vi: Đoạn E: kho chứa và công trình hành chính tập trung gần các cửa lấy nước chính.

parts.instr: Writing Task 1. You should spend about 20 minutes on this task.
parts.instrVi: Bài viết 1. Nên dành khoảng 20 phút.

items.text: The table shows the percentage of working adults in the city of Marlow who used each means of transport to travel to work in 1995, 2005 and 2015. Car: 62 percent in 1995, 55 percent in 2005, 41 percent in 2015. Bus: 18 percent, 19 percent, 21 percent. Bicycle: 4 percent, 8 percent, 17 percent. Train: 11 percent, 14 percent, 15 percent. Walking: 5 percent, 4 percent, 6 percent.
items.q: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
items.sample: The table compares the proportion of working adults in Marlow who commuted by five means of transport in 1995, 2005 and 2015. Overall, the car remained the most common choice throughout, but its dominance declined sharply, while cycling grew faster than any other mode. In 1995, the car accounted for 62 percent of journeys, more than three times the figure for buses, which stood at 18 percent. By 2005 the share of car commuters had fallen to 55 percent, and by 2015 it had dropped further to 41 percent, a fall of 21 percentage points over the two decades. The biggest rise was seen in cycling. Only 4 percent of workers rode a bicycle in 1995, but the figure doubled to 8 percent in 2005 and then more than doubled again to 17 percent in 2015, so that cycling overtook both trains and walking. Train use increased steadily from 11 percent to 15 percent, and bus use also grew slightly, from 18 percent to 21 percent. Walking was the least popular means of transport, and the proportion of walkers hardly changed, fluctuating between 4 and 6 percent. In summary, the figures suggest a clear shift away from the car toward cycling and public transport.
items.vi: Task 1: mô tả bảng số liệu, nêu xu hướng chính (xe hơi giảm, xe đạp tăng mạnh) và so sánh các phương tiện.

parts.instr: Writing Task 2. You should spend about 40 minutes on this task. Write at least 250 words.
parts.instrVi: Bài viết 2. Nên dành khoảng 40 phút. Viết ít nhất 250 từ.

items.q: Some people believe that governments should spend public money on the arts, such as museums and theaters, while others think that this money should be used for essential services such as healthcare and education. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
items.sample:
People disagree about whether public money should support the arts or be reserved for essential services. In my opinion, both sides have a point, but a balanced approach is the most sensible one.

Those who favor spending on essential services argue that governments have a basic duty to protect health, provide schools and keep citizens safe. When hospitals are overcrowded or classrooms lack teachers, funding a new gallery can seem like an irresponsible luxury. Public budgets are limited, and money spent on one area cannot be spent on another, so it is natural that voters expect the most urgent needs to come first.

However, supporters of the arts make a strong case too. Museums, theaters and libraries preserve a shared heritage and give people of every income access to culture, something that private companies would offer only to those who can pay. They also bring practical benefits. Cultural institutions attract tourists, create jobs and revive neglected city districts, so the spending is partly repaid. In addition, there is evidence that children who take part in music, drama or art programs gain confidence and perform better at school, which links the arts directly to education.

In my view, essential services must have priority, because without good health and basic education people cannot enjoy or contribute to culture at all. Nevertheless, the arts should not be dismissed as a frivolous extra. A small but stable share of public funds, supported by ticket sales and private donations, would allow cultural life to thrive without damaging more urgent services.

In conclusion, governments should first make sure that healthcare and education are properly funded, and then invest a modest, well-planned amount in the arts, since a society needs both a healthy population and a rich cultural life.
items.vi: Task 2: thảo luận hai quan điểm về chi tiêu công cho nghệ thuật và dịch vụ thiết yếu, nêu ý kiến cá nhân rõ ràng.

parts.instr: Part 1. Answer the questions about familiar topics.
parts.instrVi: Phần 1. Trả lời các câu hỏi về chủ đề quen thuộc.

items.q: Do you enjoy cooking? Why or why not?
items.sample: Yes, I really enjoy cooking, mainly because it helps me relax after a long day. I like trying new recipes at the weekend and sharing the meals with my family and friends.
items.vi: Câu trả lời mẫu: nói bạn có thích nấu ăn không, kèm lý do (thư giãn, chia sẻ với gia đình).

items.q: What did you usually eat for breakfast when you were a child?
items.sample: When I was a child, I usually had rice porridge or a bowl of noodles for breakfast, and sometimes my mother made fried eggs. It was simple food, but it kept me full until lunchtime.
items.vi: Nói về thói quen ăn sáng thời nhỏ, dùng thì quá khứ (used to / usually had).

items.q: Do you prefer eating at home or in restaurants?
items.sample: I prefer eating at home because it is cheaper and healthier, and I can choose exactly what goes into my meal. However, I enjoy going to restaurants occasionally, especially on special occasions.
items.vi: Nêu sự lựa chọn và lý do, có thể so sánh hai phương án.

items.q: How have eating habits in your country changed in recent years?
items.sample: Eating habits have changed a lot recently. People are busier, so many of them order food online or buy ready meals, but at the same time more people are interested in healthy food and eating less sugar.
items.vi: Nói về sự thay đổi thói quen ăn uống: bận rộn hơn, đặt đồ ăn online, quan tâm sức khỏe hơn.

parts.instr: Part 2. Talk about the topic on the card for one to two minutes.
parts.instrVi: Phần 2. Nói về chủ đề trên thẻ trong 1 đến 2 phút.

items.q:
Describe an interesting conversation you had with a stranger.
You should say:
- who the person was
- where and when you met
- what you talked about
and explain why you found the conversation interesting.
items.sample:
I would like to talk about a conversation I had with a stranger, an elderly man, on a long train journey last summer. I was travelling to visit my grandparents, and he sat in the seat next to mine. At first we only exchanged a few polite words, but soon he asked me what I was studying.

When I told him I was interested in engineering, he started to describe his career as a ship builder. He explained how large vessels are designed to stay stable in rough seas, and he told me several funny stories about the early days of his work. We also talked about how our town had changed over the past fifty years, because he had grown up only a few streets from where I live now.

I found the conversation interesting for two reasons. First, I learned many things that I had never read in a book. Second, it showed me that people who seem very different from us can share the same curiosity. Before we said goodbye he gave me some advice about studying hard and staying patient, and I still remember it today.
items.vi: Phần 2: nói liên tục về một cuộc trò chuyện thú vị với người lạ, theo các gợi ý trên thẻ và nêu lý do thấy thú vị.

parts.instr: Part 3. Discuss the more abstract questions related to the topic.
parts.instrVi: Phần 3. Thảo luận các câu hỏi trừu tượng liên quan đến chủ đề.

items.q: Why are some people reluctant to talk to strangers?
items.sample: Some people are reluctant because they feel shy or worry that a stranger will not want to talk. Others are concerned about safety, especially in big cities. In addition, many people now prefer to look at their phones in public, so starting a conversation feels unusual.
items.vi: Nêu lý do ngại nói chuyện với người lạ: nhút nhát, lo an toàn, thói quen dùng điện thoại.

items.q: Do you think technology has made it easier or harder to meet new people?
items.sample: In some ways it is easier, but also harder in others, because social media lets us contact people from all over the world. However, online contact is often shallow, and people may spend less time talking face to face. So I think technology gives us more chances but weaker connections.
items.vi: Nêu quan điểm công nghệ giúp dễ hay khó gặp gỡ người mới, có so sánh hai mặt.

items.q: What can people learn from talking to others of a different age or background?
items.sample: People of a different age or background can teach us new ideas and different points of view. An older person may share life experience, while a younger person may explain new trends. We learn a lot from this kind of exchange, which makes society more tolerant and helps us avoid stereotypes.
items.vi: Nêu điều học được khi trò chuyện với người khác tuổi hoặc khác hoàn cảnh.
